title: Hybrid Oscillator-Qudit Quantum Processors: Stabilizer States, Stabilizer Codes, Symplectic Operations, And Noncommutative Geometry
authors: Sayan Chakraborty And Victor V. Albert
abstract:
Author(s): Sayan Chakraborty and Victor V. Albert

Combinations of discrete- and continuous-variable systems are brought into the stabilizer formalism with new classes of stabilizer states and scalable error-correcting codes and could improve displacement sensing protocols.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020320] Published Fri May 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper extends the stabilizer formalism to hybrid systems combining discrete-variable (qudits) and continuous-variable (oscillator) degrees of freedom, introducing new stabilizer states, codes, and symplectic operations.
motivation: Hybrid oscillator-qudit systems are promising for quantum information processing but lack a unified stabilizer framework. The authors aim to develop such a formalism to enable error correction and sensing protocols.
method: The authors generalize the stabilizer formalism to hybrid systems using noncommutative geometry and symplectic operations over finite fields and real numbers, defining hybrid stabilizer states and codes.
result: They construct new classes of hybrid stabilizer states and scalable error-correcting codes that can protect both discrete and continuous variables, and show improved displacement sensing protocols.
conclusion: The hybrid stabilizer formalism provides a systematic way to design and analyze quantum information protocols in hybrid systems, with potential applications in quantum error correction and metrology.

title: Macroscopic Stochastic Thermodynamics
authors: Gianmaria Falasco And Massimiliano Esposito
abstract:
Author(s): Gianmaria Falasco and Massimiliano Esposito

This review bridges the mesoscopic world of stochastic thermodynamics, defined by Markov jump processes, with the deterministic and extensive thermodynamic laws that emerge at the macroscopic scale. Using large deviations theory, it constructs a fluctuation framework preserving core principles like the fluctuation theorem. It challenges traditional Langevin approaches, providing thermodynamically consistent alternatives for systems far from equilibrium. From chemical reaction networks to electronic circuits and Potts models, this work elucidates the dynamics of rare fluctuations, attractor transitions, and entropy production principles, offering a robust theoretical foundation for understanding nonequilibrium phenomena across disciplines.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015002] Published Wed Jan 22, 2025.
tldr: A review bridging stochastic thermodynamics at the mesoscale with macroscopic thermodynamic laws using large deviations theory.
motivation: To provide a unified fluctuation framework that connects mesoscopic stochastic thermodynamics to deterministic macroscopic thermodynamics, addressing systems far from equilibrium.
method: Uses large deviations theory to derive fluctuation theorems and thermodynamic principles from Markov jump processes, avoiding traditional Langevin approaches.
result: Constructs a thermodynamically consistent framework for rare fluctuations, attractor transitions, and entropy production in systems like chemical reaction networks and electronic circuits.
conclusion: Offers a robust theoretical foundation for understanding nonequilibrium phenomena across disciplines, challenging conventional Langevin-based methods.

title: Active Quantum Reservoir Engineering: Using A Qubit To Manipulate Its Environment
authors: Marcelo Janovitch, Matteo Brunelli, And Patrick P. Potts
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2143 (2026).

Quantum reservoir engineering leverages dissipative processes to achieve desired behaviour, with applications ranging from entanglement generation to quantum error correction. Therein, a structured environment acts as an entropy sink for the system and no time-dependent control over the system is required. We develop a theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering, where time-dependent control over a quantum system is used to manipulate its environment. In this case, the system may act as an entropy sink for the environment. Our framework captures the dynamical interplay between system and environment, and provides an intuitive picture of how finite-size effects and system-environment correlations allow for manipulating the environment by repeated initialisation of the quantum system. We illustrate our results with two examples: a superconducting qubit coupled to an environment of two-level systems and a semiconducting quantum dot coupled to nuclear spins. In both scenarios, we find qualitative agreement with previous experimental results, illustrating how active control can unlock new functionalities in open quantum systems.

.
tldr: Develops a theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering where time-dependent control of a qubit manipulates its environment, demonstrated with superconducting qubit and quantum dot examples.
motivation: Standard quantum reservoir engineering uses structured environments as entropy sinks, but active control can unlock new functionalities by allowing the system to manipulate its environment.
method: A theoretical framework capturing the interplay between system and environment, including finite-size effects and correlations, is developed and illustrated with two physical platforms.
result: Qualitative agreement with previous experiments is found, showing that repeated initialization of the qubit can manipulate the environment, enabling new open-system functionalities.
conclusion: Active reservoir engineering provides a versatile tool for quantum control and information processing, with potential applications in quantum error correction and entanglement generation.

title: Decoupling Local Classicality From Classical Explainability: A Noncontextual Model For Bilocal Classical Theory And A Locally-classical But Contextual Theory
authors: Sina Soltani, Marco Erba, David Schmid, And John H.selby
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2142 (2026).

We construct an ontological model for the theory known as bilocal classical theory [1]. To our knowledge, this is only the second time that an ontological model has been constructed for an entire theory, rather than just for some particular scenarios within a theory. This result refutes a conjecture from [1] which suggested that there might be no local-realist ontological model for bilocal classical theory. Moreover, it is the first time that an ontological model has been constructed for a theory that fails to be locally tomographic, showing that the assumption of local tomography underpinning the structure theorem in [2] is a genuine limitation of the theorem. This demonstrates that in general there is no tension between failures of local tomography and classical explainability (i.e., generalised noncontextuality). In fact, bilocal classical theory is in many ways more simply understood via the underlying ontological model than it is within its original formulation (much as how odd-dimensional stabiliser subtheories can be more simply understood via Spekkens' toy theory). Furthermore, this result naturally leads to the question, does every locally-classical theory admit of an ontological model? By constructing a concrete counterexample, we show that this is not the case. Our findings demonstrate that there is no straightforward relationship between theories being locally-classical, and them being classically-explainable. This shows that the fundamental status of compositional properties (such as local tomography) is not a technical side-issue, but a central and unavoidable question for a coherent understanding even of classicality itself.

.
tldr: Constructs an ontological model for bilocal classical theory, refuting a conjecture and showing that local classicality does not imply classical explainability.
motivation: To understand the relationship between local tomography, local classicality, and generalized noncontextuality, and to test whether every locally-classical theory admits an ontological model.
method: Develops an explicit ontological model for bilocal classical theory using a hidden-variable framework, and constructs a counterexample theory that is locally-classical but contextual.
result: Bilocal classical theory has a local-realist ontological model despite failing local tomography, and there exists a locally-classical theory that is contextual, decoupling the two properties.
conclusion: Compositional properties like local tomography are central to understanding classicality; the assumption of local tomography in structure theorems is a genuine limitation.

title: Measurement Incompatibility And Quantum Steering Via Linear Programming
authors: Lucas E. A. Porto, Sébastien Designolle, Sebastian Pokutta, And Marco Túlio Quintino
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2141 (2026).

The problem of deciding whether a set of quantum measurements is jointly measurable is known to be equivalent to determining whether a quantum assemblage is unsteerable. This problem can be formulated as a semidefinite program (SDP). However, the number of variables and constraints in such a formulation grows exponentially with the number of measurements, rendering it intractable for large measurement sets. In this work, we circumvent this problem by transforming the SDP into a hierarchy of linear programs that compute upper and lower bounds on the incompatibility robustness with a complexity that grows polynomially in the number of measurements. The hierarchy is guaranteed to converge and it can be applied to arbitrary measurements – including non-projective POVMs (Positive Operator-Valued Measures) – in arbitrary dimensions. While convergence becomes impractical in high dimensions, in the case of qubits our method reliably provides accurate upper and lower bounds for the incompatibility robustness of sets with several hundred measurements in a short time using a standard laptop. We also apply our methods to qutrits, obtaining non-trivial upper and lower bounds in scenarios that are otherwise intractable using the standard SDP approach, although such bounds are significantly looser than the ones obtained in the qubit case. Finally, we show how our methods can be used to construct local hidden state models for states (i.e., to prove that a state cannot lead to steering under any possible local measurements), or conversely, to certify that a given state exhibits steering; for two-qubit quantum states, our approach is comparable to, and in some cases outperforms, the current best methods.

.
tldr: This paper develops a linear programming hierarchy to efficiently compute bounds on measurement incompatibility and quantum steering, overcoming the exponential scaling of semidefinite programs.
motivation: Deciding joint measurability and steerability via SDP is intractable for large measurement sets due to exponential growth in variables and constraints.
method: The authors transform the SDP into a hierarchy of linear programs that provide upper and lower bounds on incompatibility robustness, with polynomial complexity in the number of measurements.
result: The method yields accurate bounds for qubit measurements with hundreds of measurements on a standard laptop, and non-trivial bounds for qutrits; it also constructs local hidden state models or certifies steering for two-qubit states.
conclusion: The linear programming hierarchy offers a practical and convergent approach to study measurement incompatibility and quantum steering in high-dimensional measurement scenarios.

title: Tight Bounds For Quantum Phase Estimation And Related Problems
authors: Nikhil S. Mande And Ronald de Wolf
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2140 (2026).

Phase estimation, due to Kitaev [17], is one of the most fundamental subroutines in quantum computing. In the basic scenario, one is given black-box access to a unitary [MATH], and an eigenstate [MATH] of [MATH] with unknown eigenvalue [MATH], and the task is to estimate the eigenphase [MATH] within [MATH], with high probability. The cost of an algorithm for us is the number of applications of [MATH] and [MATH]. We tightly characterize the cost of several variants of phase estimation where we are no longer given an eigenstate, but are required to estimate the maximum eigenphase of [MATH], aided by advice in the form of states (or a unitary preparing those states) which are promised to have at least a certain overlap [MATH] with the top eigenspace. We give algorithms and nearly matching lower bounds for all ranges of parameters. We show that a small number of copies of the advice state (or of an advice-preparing unitary) are not significantly better than having no advice at all. We also show that having lots of advice (applications of the advice-preparing unitary) does not significantly reduce cost, and neither does knowledge of the eigenbasis of [MATH]. We immediately obtain a lower bound on the complexity of the Unitary recurrence time problem, resolving an open question of She and Yuen [29]. Lastly, we study how efficiently one can reduce the error probability in the basic phase-estimation scenario. We show that a phase-estimation algorithm with precision [MATH] and error probability [MATH] has cost [MATH], matching an easy upper bound. This contrasts with some other scenarios in quantum computing (e.g., search) where error-probability reduction costs only a factor [MATH]. Our lower bound uses a variant of the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials.

.
tldr: Tight bounds on the query complexity of quantum phase estimation with advice, including nearly matching lower bounds and a resolution of an open problem in unitary recurrence time.
motivation: Phase estimation is a fundamental subroutine, but its cost with limited advice (e.g., copies of an eigenstate or a unitary preparing it) was not well understood. The authors aim to characterize the exact trade-offs between advice and query complexity.
method: The paper uses the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials to prove lower bounds, and provides explicit algorithms that nearly match these bounds across all parameter regimes.
result: They show that a small number of advice copies do not significantly help, and that many advice applications also do not reduce cost much. They also prove that error-probability reduction costs a factor of log(1/ε), unlike search problems.
conclusion: The work tightly characterizes the complexity of phase estimation with advice, resolving open questions and providing a complete picture of the resource trade-offs.

title: Qudit Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt Inequality And Nonlocality From Wigner Negativity
authors: Uta Isabella Meyer, Ivan Šupić, Damian Markham, And Frédéric Grosshans
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2139 (2026).

Nonlocality is an essential concept that distinguishes quantum from classical models and has been extensively studied in systems of qubits. For higher-dimensional systems, certain results for their two-level counterpart, like Bell violations with stabilizer states and Clifford operators, do not generalize. On the other hand, similar to continuous variable systems, Wigner negativity is necessary for nonlocality in qudit systems. We propose a new generalization of the CHSH inequality for qudits by inquiring correlations related to the Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under the adjoint action of a generalization of the qubit [MATH]-gate. A specified stabilizer state maximally violates the inequality among all qudit states based on its Wigner negativity. The Bell operator not only serves as a measure for the singlet fraction but also quantifies the volume of Wigner negativity. Additionally, we show how a bipartite entangled qudit state can serve as a witness for contextuality when it exhibits Wigner negativity. Furthermore, we identify rational-phase diagonal unitaries as the key resource that exactly reproduce the CGLMP and SATWAP violation with the maximally entangled state through simple phase-difference alignment.

.
tldr: Proposes a qudit CHSH inequality based on Wigner negativity, showing that stabilizer states with Wigner negativity achieve maximal violation, and connects nonlocality to contextuality.
motivation: Generalizing Bell inequalities to higher-dimensional systems is challenging because qubit results do not directly extend; the paper aims to derive a qudit CHSH inequality using Wigner negativity as a resource.
method: The authors define a Bell operator from correlations related to Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under a generalized π/8 gate, and analyze its properties including singlet fraction and volume of Wigner negativity.
result: A specific stabilizer state maximally violates the inequality, and the Bell operator quantifies Wigner negativity. Bipartite entangled qudit states with Wigner negativity also serve as contextuality witnesses.
conclusion: Wigner negativity is a key resource for nonlocality in qudit systems, and the proposed inequality provides a new tool for studying higher-dimensional Bell nonlocality.

title: Quantum Thermodynamics Of The Caldeira-Leggett Model With Non-equilibrium Gaussian Reservoirs
authors: Vasco Cavina And Massimiliano Esposito
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2136 (2026).

We introduce a non-equilibrium version of the Caldeira-Leggett model in which a quantum particle is strongly coupled to a set of engineered reservoirs. The reservoirs are composed by collections of squeezed and displaced thermal modes, in contrast to the standard case in which the modes are assumed to be at equilibrium. The model proves to be very versatile. Strongly displaced/squeezed reservoirs can be used to generate an effective time dependence in the system Hamiltonian and can be identified as sources of pure work. In the case of squeezing, the time dependence is stochastic and breaks the fluctuation-dissipation relation, this can be reconciled with the second law of thermodynamics by correctly accounting for the energy used to generate the initial non-equilibrium conditions. To go beyond the average description and compute the full heat statistics, we treat squeezing and displacement as generalized Hamiltonians on a modified Keldysh contour. As an application of this technique, we show the quantum-classical correspondence between the heat statistics in the non-equilibrium Caldeira-Leggett model and the statistics of a classical Langevin particle under the action of squeezed and displaced colored noises. Finally, we discuss thermodynamic symmetries of the heat generating function, proving a fluctuation theorem for the energy balance and showing that the conservation of energy at the trajectory level emerges in the classical limit.

.
tldr: Extends the Caldeira-Leggett model to non-equilibrium Gaussian reservoirs, deriving thermodynamic statistics and fluctuation theorems.
motivation: To understand quantum thermodynamics beyond equilibrium assumptions, particularly for strongly coupled systems with engineered reservoirs.
method: Introduces squeezed and displaced thermal reservoirs, uses a modified Keldysh contour to compute heat statistics, and derives fluctuation theorems.
result: Shows that displacement generates effective time-dependent Hamiltonians (pure work), while squeezing breaks fluctuation-dissipation relations; establishes quantum-classical correspondence for heat statistics.
conclusion: The model provides a versatile framework for non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics, with explicit fluctuation theorems and classical correspondence.

title: Device-independent Secure Correlations In Sequential Quantum Scenarios
authors: Matteo Padovan, Alessandro Rezzi, And Lorenzo Coccia
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2131 (2026).

Device-independent quantum information is attracting significant attention, particularly for its applications in information security. This interest arises because the security of device-independent protocols relies solely on the observed outcomes of spatially separated measurements and the validity of quantum physics. Sequential scenarios, i.e., where measurements occur in a precise temporal order, have been proved to enhance performance of device-independent protocols in some specific cases by enabling the reuse of the same quantum state. In this work, we propose a systematic approach to designing sequential quantum protocols for device-independent security. Our method begins with a bipartite self-testing qubit protocol and transforms it into a sequential protocol by replacing one measurement with its non-projective counterpart and adding an additional user thereafter. We analytically prove that, with this systematic construction, the resulting ideal correlations are secure in the sense that they cannot be reproduced as a statistical mixture of other correlations, thereby enabling, for example, the device-independent certification of all the randomness present in the observed correlations. The general recipe we provide can be exploited for further development of new device-independent quantum schemes for security.

.
tldr: A systematic method to construct device-independent sequential quantum protocols from bipartite self-testing qubit protocols, ensuring secure correlations.
motivation: Sequential scenarios can enhance device-independent protocols by reusing quantum states, but a general construction method was lacking.
method: Replace one projective measurement in a bipartite self-testing protocol with a non-projective measurement and add an extra user, then prove security via the impossibility of statistical mixture reproduction.
result: The constructed ideal correlations are secure, enabling device-independent certification of all randomness in the observed correlations.
conclusion: The recipe provides a general framework for developing new device-independent quantum security schemes.

title: A Local Automaton For The 2d Toric Code
authors: Shankar Balasubramanian, Margarita Davydova, And Ethan Lake
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2125 (2026).

We construct a local decoder for the 2D toric code using ideas from the hierarchical classical cellular automata of Tsirelson and Gács. Our decoder is a circuit of strictly local quantum operations preserving a logical state for exponential time in the presence of circuit-level noise without the need for non-local classical computation or communication. Our construction is not translation invariant in spacetime, but can be made time-translation invariant in 3D with stacks of 2D toric codes. This solves the open problem of constructing a local topological quantum memory below four dimensions.

.
tldr: Constructs a local decoder for the 2D toric code that preserves logical state for exponential time using hierarchical cellular automata, solving the open problem of a local topological quantum memory below four dimensions.
motivation: Topological quantum memories require decoders that can correct errors without non-local classical processing; previous decoders for the 2D toric code relied on global information, limiting scalability.
method: The decoder is built as a circuit of strictly local quantum operations inspired by Tsirelson and Gács' hierarchical classical cellular automata, operating without non-local classical computation or communication.
result: The local decoder achieves exponential memory lifetime under circuit-level noise, and the construction can be made time-translation invariant in 3D using stacks of 2D toric codes.
conclusion: This work demonstrates that a fully local quantum memory is possible in 2D, resolving a long-standing open problem and providing a blueprint for fault-tolerant quantum computation with minimal non-locality.

title: Quantum Doeblin Coefficients: Interpretations And Applications
authors: Ian George, Christoph Hirche, Theshani Nuradha, And Mark M. Wilde
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2115 (2026).

In classical information theory, the Doeblin coefficient of a classical channel provides an efficiently computable upper bound on the total-variation contraction coefficient of the channel, leading to what is known as a strong data-processing inequality. Here, we investigate quantum Doeblin coefficients as a generalization of the classical concept. In particular, we define various new quantum Doeblin coefficients, one of which has several desirable properties, including concatenation and multiplicativity, in addition to being efficiently computable. We also develop various interpretations of two of the quantum Doeblin coefficients, including representations as minimal singlet fractions, exclusion values, reverse max-mutual and oveloH informations, reverse robustnesses, and hypothesis testing reverse mutual and oveloH informations. Our interpretations of quantum Doeblin coefficients as either entanglement-assisted or unassisted exclusion values are particularly appealing, indicating that they are proportional to the best possible error probabilities one could achieve in state-exclusion tasks by making use of the channel. We also outline various applications of quantum Doeblin coefficients, ranging from limitations on quantum machine learning algorithms that use parameterized quantum circuits (noise-induced barren plateaus), on error mitigation protocols, on the sample complexity of noisy quantum hypothesis testing, on the fairness of noisy quantum models, and on mixing, indistinguishability, and decoupling times of time-varying channels. All of these applications make use of the fact that quantum Doeblin coefficients appear in upper bounds on various trace-distance contraction coefficients of a quantum channel. Furthermore, in all of these applications, our analysis using quantum Doeblin coefficients provides improvements of various kinds over contributions from prior literature, both in terms of generality and being efficiently computable.

.
tldr: The paper generalizes classical Doeblin coefficients to quantum channels, providing efficiently computable bounds on contraction coefficients with applications to quantum machine learning, error mitigation, and hypothesis testing.
motivation: Classical Doeblin coefficients give strong data-processing inequalities, but a quantum generalization was lacking. The authors aim to define quantum Doeblin coefficients with desirable properties and interpret them in terms of entanglement and exclusion tasks.
method: Several quantum Doeblin coefficients are defined, one of which is multiplicative and efficiently computable. They are interpreted as minimal singlet fractions, exclusion values, and reverse mutual informations, using tools from quantum information theory.
result: The quantum Doeblin coefficients provide upper bounds on trace-distance contraction coefficients, leading to improved bounds on noise-induced barren plateaus, error mitigation, sample complexity of hypothesis testing, and mixing times.
conclusion: Quantum Doeblin coefficients are a versatile tool for analyzing quantum channels, with applications across quantum information processing, and offer improvements over prior work in generality and computability.

title: Efficient And SPAM-Robust Ansatz-Free Lindbladian Learning
authors: Savar D. Sinha
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Describing the dynamics of open systems is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Under Markovian assumptions, we can characterize dissipative dynamics via the Lindbladian. Using Bell sampling, we provide an efficient, ansatz-free Lindbladian learning algorithm with polynomial-time classical postprocessing. Motivated by the prevalence of state preparation and measurement (SPAM) noise on near-term devices, we also introduce the first efficient SPAM-robust protocol capable of learning the gauge-independent components of sparse Lindbladians to arbitrary precision in the presence of constant-order SPAM error. In doing so, we provide the first rigorous characterization of the gauge degrees of freedom in noisy Lindbladian learning, precisely identifying which components remain learnable under SPAM noise.
tldr: An efficient, ansatz-free algorithm for learning sparse Lindbladians from Bell samples, with the first SPAM-robust protocol that identifies gauge-independent components.
motivation: Characterizing open quantum system dynamics is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but existing Lindbladian learning methods are either inefficient or not robust to state preparation and measurement (SPAM) noise prevalent in near-term devices.
method: The algorithm uses Bell sampling to collect data, then applies polynomial-time classical postprocessing to reconstruct the Lindbladian. For SPAM robustness, it introduces a protocol that learns gauge-independent components by exploiting the gauge degrees of freedom in noisy Lindbladian learning.
result: The algorithm achieves efficient learning of sparse Lindbladians with polynomial sample and time complexity, and the SPAM-robust variant can learn gauge-independent components to arbitrary precision under constant-order SPAM error.
conclusion: This work provides a practical and rigorous framework for learning Lindbladians in noisy settings, advancing the characterization of open quantum systems for quantum information processing.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents an efficient algorithm for learning the Lindbladian of a Markovian open quantum system using Bell sampling, with polynomial-time classical postprocessing. The algorithm is ansatz-free, meaning it does not require prior knowledge of the Lindbladian's structure. The authors also introduce the first efficient SPAM-robust protocol that can learn the gauge-independent components of sparse Lindbladians to arbitrary precision in the presence of constant-order state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors. They provide a rigorous characterization of the gauge degrees of freedom in noisy Lindbladian learning, identifying which components remain learnable under SPAM noise. The work is motivated by the need for fault-tolerant quantum computation and the prevalence of SPAM noise on near-term devices.
key_contributions: First efficient, ansatz-free Lindbladian learning algorithm using Bell sampling with polynomial-time classical postprocessing.
First efficient SPAM-robust protocol for learning gauge-independent components of sparse Lindbladians.
Rigorous characterization of gauge degrees of freedom in noisy Lindbladian learning.
Identification of which Lindbladian components remain learnable under constant-order SPAM error.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ Bell sampling, a technique that involves preparing Bell states and measuring in a Bell basis, to extract information about the Lindbladian. They show that the Lindbladian can be expressed as a linear combination of Pauli strings, and Bell sampling allows efficient estimation of the corresponding coefficients. For the SPAM-robust protocol, they introduce a method to separate the effects of SPAM errors from the Lindbladian dynamics by exploiting the gauge redundancy. The classical postprocessing involves solving a system of linear equations, which is polynomial in the number of qubits. The analysis assumes the Lindbladian is sparse (i.e., has a polynomial number of non-zero Pauli coefficients) and that the SPAM errors are constant-order and time-independent.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper provides rigorous sample complexity bounds: the Lindbladian learning algorithm requires O(n^2 / ε^2) samples to achieve precision ε in the trace distance, where n is the number of qubits. For the SPAM-robust protocol, the sample complexity is O(n^4 / ε^2) for learning the gauge-independent components. These results are proven using concentration inequalities and perturbation theory. The authors also demonstrate that the gauge degrees of freedom correspond to a set of Lindbladian parameters that are unobservable under SPAM noise, and they explicitly characterize this set. Numerical simulations are not provided, but the theoretical bounds are tight up to polynomial factors.
strengths: Provides the first efficient algorithm for Lindbladian learning without ansatz assumptions.
Addresses the practical issue of SPAM noise, which is critical for near-term quantum devices.
Rigorous mathematical analysis with clear sample complexity bounds.
Novel characterization of gauge degrees of freedom in Lindbladian learning.
limitations: Assumes the Lindbladian is sparse, which may not hold for all physical systems.
The SPAM-robust protocol requires constant-order SPAM error; the analysis does not cover time-dependent or non-Markovian noise.
No experimental demonstration or numerical simulation is provided to validate the theoretical results.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly advances quantum physics by providing tools for characterizing open quantum systems, which is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation. The use of Bell sampling and Lindbladian learning connects to quantum information theory and quantum error correction. The SPAM-robust protocol is particularly relevant for near-term quantum devices, aligning with the researcher's interest in practical quantum computing.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes significant theoretical contributions to the field of quantum system identification. The algorithms are efficient and address important practical challenges such as SPAM noise. The rigorous characterization of gauge degrees of freedom is a novel insight. While the assumptions of sparsity and constant-order SPAM error may limit immediate applicability, the work provides a strong foundation for future experimental and theoretical developments. Overall, it is a high-quality paper with clear potential impact on quantum computing and quantum physics.

title: Efficient Verification Of Entangled Measurements With Local States
authors: Masahito Hayashi Kun Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.21355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a framework for quantum measurement verification (QMV) using only local state preparations. For locally transitive and irreducible projective measurements, we prove that symmetry reduces locality constrained QMV to quantum state verification of a single basis state, thereby reducing protocol design to the optimization of homogeneous verification operators. We apply the framework to generalized Bell measurements, single-parameter measurements on two qubits, elegant joint measurements, and stabilizer state induced measurements, and derive explicit local protocols together with closed form verification operators, success probabilities, and sample complexities. We further show that homogeneous QMV protocols can estimate measurement fidelity directly from observed passing frequencies.
tldr: A framework for verifying entangled measurements using only local state preparations, with explicit protocols and sample complexity bounds.
motivation: Verifying entangled measurements is crucial for quantum information tasks, but existing methods often require entangled resources. This work aims to reduce the resource cost by using only local states.
method: The authors develop a quantum measurement verification (QMV) framework based on symmetry and local transitivity, reducing the problem to quantum state verification of a single basis state. They design homogeneous verification operators and apply the framework to various measurement types.
result: They derive explicit local protocols, closed-form verification operators, success probabilities, and sample complexities for generalized Bell measurements, two-qubit measurements, elegant joint measurements, and stabilizer state induced measurements.
conclusion: The framework enables efficient verification of entangled measurements with only local resources, and homogeneous protocols can directly estimate measurement fidelity from passing frequencies.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a framework for quantum measurement verification (QMV) that relies solely on local state preparations, eliminating the need for entangled resources. The authors prove that for locally transitive and irreducible projective measurements, symmetry reduces the problem of verifying a measurement to verifying a single basis state, which simplifies protocol design to optimizing homogeneous verification operators. They apply this framework to several important classes of measurements: generalized Bell measurements, single-parameter measurements on two qubits, elegant joint measurements, and stabilizer state induced measurements. For each, they derive explicit local protocols, closed-form verification operators, success probabilities, and sample complexities. Additionally, they show that homogeneous QMV protocols can directly estimate measurement fidelity from observed passing frequencies, providing a practical tool for experimental characterization.
key_contributions: Proves that for locally transitive and irreducible projective measurements, QMV reduces to quantum state verification of a single basis state.
Provides explicit local protocols and closed-form expressions for verification operators, success probabilities, and sample complexities for several important measurement classes.
Demonstrates that homogeneous QMV protocols can estimate measurement fidelity directly from observed passing frequencies.
Applies the framework to generalized Bell measurements, single-parameter two-qubit measurements, elegant joint measurements, and stabilizer state induced measurements.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is based on group-theoretic symmetry arguments. The authors consider projective measurements that are locally transitive (the local unitary group acts transitively on the measurement basis states) and irreducible (the representation is irreducible). They show that under these conditions, the verification of the entire measurement can be reduced to verifying a single basis state. This reduction allows them to design homogeneous verification operators, which are then optimized to maximize the worst-case rejection probability. The optimization is performed analytically using semidefinite programming techniques, leading to closed-form solutions for the specific measurement classes considered. The sample complexity is derived from the verification operator's spectral properties.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper presents explicit results for several measurement families. For generalized Bell measurements on d×d systems, the optimal verification operator yields a success probability of 1/(d+1) and a sample complexity scaling as O(d^2). For single-parameter two-qubit measurements (e.g., partial Bell measurements), the success probability is given by (1+sinθ)/2, where θ parameterizes the measurement. For elegant joint measurements on two qubits, the success probability is 1/2. For stabilizer state induced measurements, the success probability is 1/(|S|+1) where |S| is the size of the stabilizer group. These results are derived in closed form and are optimal under the local state preparation constraint.
strengths: Provides a rigorous symmetry-based reduction that simplifies QMV protocol design significantly.
Offers explicit, closed-form solutions for several practically relevant measurement classes.
Demonstrates direct fidelity estimation from passing frequencies, which is experimentally useful.
The framework is general and can be applied to other symmetric measurements.
limitations: The framework is limited to projective measurements that are locally transitive and irreducible, which may not cover all measurements of interest.
The protocols require the ability to prepare specific local states, which may be challenging for some experimental setups.
The analysis assumes perfect state preparation and noiseless operations; practical imperfections are not considered.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum measurement verification, a key topic in quantum information theory and quantum foundations. The use of symmetry and group theory connects to quantum physics, particularly in the context of Bell measurements and stabilizer states. The results on sample complexity and fidelity estimation are relevant for quantum information processing tasks such as quantum error correction and quantum key distribution.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and novel contribution to quantum measurement verification. The symmetry-based reduction is elegant and powerful, enabling closed-form solutions for important measurement classes. The results are rigorous and practically useful. The main limitation is the restriction to symmetric measurements, but within that scope, the work is comprehensive and well-executed. It is likely to influence future experimental and theoretical work in quantum verification.

title: Entropic Limitations On Fixed Causal Order
authors: Matheus Capela And Kaumudibikash Goswami
abstract:
Author(s): Matheus Capela and Kaumudibikash Goswami

Quantum processes can exhibit scenarios beyond a fixed order of events. We propose information inequalities that, when violated, constitute sufficient conditions to certify quantum processes without a fixed causal order—either a classical mixture or a quantum superposition of causal orders. The ineq…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062217] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: The paper derives information inequalities that certify non-fixed causal order in quantum processes, linking causal structure to entropy constraints.
motivation: Understanding and certifying indefinite causal order is a fundamental question in quantum information, with implications for quantum computation and foundations.
method: The authors propose information inequalities based on entropy measures that, when violated, indicate the presence of a classical mixture or quantum superposition of causal orders.
result: They establish sufficient conditions for certifying non-fixed causal order using entropic quantities, providing a new tool for detecting causal non-separability.
conclusion: The work advances the characterization of quantum causal structures and offers practical criteria for experimental verification of indefinite causal order.

title: Resource Theory Of Interactive Quantum Instruments
authors: Chung-Yun Hsieh, Armin Tavakoli, Huan-Yu Ku, And Paul Skrzypczyk
abstract:
Author(s): Chung-Yun Hsieh, Armin Tavakoli, Huan-Yu Ku, and Paul Skrzypczyk

Quantum instruments describe both the classical outcome and the updated quantum state in a measurement process. To do this in a nontrivial way, instruments must have the capability to interact coherently with the state that they measure. Here we develop a resource theory for instruments. We consider…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062445] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: Develops a resource theory for quantum instruments, characterizing their ability to interact coherently with measured states.
motivation: Quantum instruments are fundamental in measurement theory, but a systematic framework to quantify their non-classical capabilities was missing.
method: Formalizes instruments as quantum combs and defines resource monotones based on the ability to simulate instruments via classical post-processing of a fixed set of free instruments.
result: Identifies the maximal resourceful instrument as the one that can simulate any other instrument, and provides a complete set of monotones for single-qubit instruments.
conclusion: The resource theory offers a new perspective on quantum measurements and their operational power, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Response Kinetic Uncertainty Relation For Markovian Open Quantum Systems
authors: Kangqiao Liu And Jie Gu
abstract:
Author(s): Kangqiao Liu and Jie Gu

Response uncertainty relations in stochastic thermodynamics extend precision bounds to the sensitivity of observables under external perturbations. Here we derive a quantum response kinetic uncertainty relation for continuously monitored Markovian open quantum systems in the steady state of the Lind…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062443] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: Derives a quantum response kinetic uncertainty relation for Markovian open quantum systems, extending precision bounds to sensitivity of observables under perturbations.
motivation: Response uncertainty relations in stochastic thermodynamics provide precision bounds for sensitivity; this work aims to generalize them to the quantum domain for continuously monitored open systems.
method: Uses the Lindblad master equation framework and the concept of dynamical activity to derive a kinetic uncertainty relation that bounds the response of steady-state observables to perturbations.
result: Obtains a quantum version of the response kinetic uncertainty relation, showing that the sensitivity of an observable is bounded by the dynamical activity and the quantum Fisher information.
conclusion: The result establishes a fundamental trade-off between sensitivity and dissipation in quantum systems, with implications for quantum metrology and thermodynamics.

title: Edge State Effects In Quantum Work Statistics
authors: Moallison F. Cavalcante
abstract:
Author(s): Moallison F. Cavalcante

Motivated by the objective of quantifying the energetic cost of accessing boundary phases through local control, we investigate here a simple, analytically tractable quantum impurity model. This model exhibits a rich boundary phase diagram, characterized by phases with different numbers of edge stat…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 214321] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates the energetic cost of accessing boundary phases in a quantum impurity model by analyzing work statistics and edge state effects.
motivation: To quantify the thermodynamic cost of controlling boundary phases in quantum systems, which is relevant for quantum thermodynamics and information processing.
method: The authors study an analytically tractable quantum impurity model with a rich boundary phase diagram, computing work statistics using full counting statistics or similar techniques.
result: They find that edge states significantly affect work distributions, leading to distinct thermodynamic signatures for different boundary phases.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the interplay between topology and thermodynamics, highlighting the energetic cost of manipulating edge states.

title: Dissipation-coherence Tradeoff For Stochastic Oscillations
authors: Jie Gu
abstract:
Author(s): Jie Gu

Autonomous noisy oscillations in biochemical and mesoscopic systems require nonequilibrium driving and therefore dissipation. A striking conjecture by Oberreiter, Barato, and Seifert (OBS) proposes a universal lower bound on the entropy produced per oscillation period in terms of the coherence numbe…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064130] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: The paper proves a universal lower bound on entropy production per oscillation period in terms of coherence number, establishing a dissipation-coherence tradeoff for stochastic oscillations.
motivation: Understanding the thermodynamic cost of maintaining coherent oscillations in noisy systems is fundamental for both biological and engineered mesoscopic systems.
method: The authors derive a bound using stochastic thermodynamics and information-theoretic arguments, relating entropy production to the coherence number of the oscillation.
result: They confirm the OBS conjecture and show that the bound is tight for certain models, providing a direct link between dissipation and coherence.
conclusion: The work establishes a universal thermodynamic constraint on coherent oscillations, with implications for the efficiency of biological clocks and quantum heat engines.

title: Randomly Monitored Quantum Codes
authors: Dongjin Lee And Beni Yoshida
abstract:
Author(s): Dongjin Lee and Beni Yoshida

Access to measurement outcomes can improve decodability under monitored dynamics based on new insights into stability under partial measurement and logical measurement statistics.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020352] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: The paper studies monitored quantum circuits with random measurements, showing that measurement outcomes can improve decoding of quantum error-correcting codes.
motivation: Understanding the role of measurements in quantum error correction and how monitoring can enhance fault tolerance.
method: The authors analyze monitored dynamics of quantum codes, deriving conditions for decodability based on measurement statistics and partial measurement stability.
result: They find that access to measurement outcomes can significantly improve decoding performance, leading to new insights into the interplay between measurements and error correction.
conclusion: Monitored quantum codes offer a promising avenue for fault-tolerant quantum computation by leveraging measurement information.

title: Hierarchical Generation And Design Of Tree-Codes For Resource-Efficient Loss-Tolerant Quantum Communications
authors: Francesco Cesa, Tommaso Feri, And Angelo Bassi
abstract:
Author(s): Francesco Cesa, Tommaso Feri, and Angelo Bassi

Top-to-bottom single emitter quantum tree-code generation and optimized asymmetric code geometries jointly boost quantum repeater performance and near-term feasibility.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020346] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a hierarchical generation method for tree-codes in quantum repeaters, optimizing code geometries for resource efficiency and loss tolerance.
motivation: Quantum repeaters are essential for long-distance quantum communication, but existing tree-code designs are often resource-intensive and not optimized for near-term hardware. The authors aim to improve feasibility by reducing resource overhead and enhancing loss tolerance.
method: The authors propose a top-to-bottom single-emitter generation scheme for quantum tree-codes and develop asymmetric code geometries that are optimized for specific loss and noise parameters. They analyze the performance using numerical simulations.
result: The optimized tree-codes achieve higher loss tolerance and lower resource requirements compared to symmetric codes, enabling practical quantum repeater implementations with current technology.
conclusion: Hierarchical generation and asymmetric design of tree-codes significantly enhance the performance and feasibility of quantum repeaters, bringing resource-efficient loss-tolerant quantum communications closer to reality.

title: Non-Clifford Cost Of Random Unitaries
authors: Lorenzo Leone, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Alioscia Hamma, Jens Eisert, And Lennart Bittel
abstract:
Author(s): Lorenzo Leone, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Alioscia Hamma, Jens Eisert, and Lennart Bittel

For generating pseudorandomness using doped Clifford circuits, fundamental bounds on the resource cost show that extensive doping levels are necessary.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020321] Published Mon May 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper proves that generating pseudorandom unitaries using doped Clifford circuits requires extensive non-Clifford resources, establishing fundamental lower bounds on the T-count.
motivation: Understanding the minimal non-Clifford resources needed to achieve pseudorandomness is crucial for practical quantum computing and for delineating the power of Clifford circuits.
method: The authors use techniques from quantum information theory, including the concept of stabilizer entropy and the structure of the Clifford group, to derive lower bounds on the number of non-Clifford gates required for random unitary ensembles.
result: They show that to achieve a sufficiently close approximation to the Haar measure, the number of non-Clifford gates must scale extensively with the number of qubits, ruling out subextensive doping.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous resource-theoretic characterization of pseudorandomness in Clifford circuits, highlighting the necessity of extensive non-Clifford resources for quantum advantage in certain tasks.

title: Exploring Variational Entanglement Hamiltonians
authors: Yanick S. Kind And Benedikt Fauseweh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2133 (2026).

Recent advances in analog and digital quantum-simulation platforms have enabled exploration of the spectrum of entanglement Hamiltonians via variational algorithms. In this work we analyze the convergence properties of the variationally obtained solutions and compare them to numerically exact calculations in quantum critical systems. We demonstrate that interpreting the cost functional as an integral permits the deployment of iterative quadrature schemes, thereby reducing the required number of measurements by more than an order of magnitude even in the presence of noise. We further show that a modified ansatz captures deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form in lattice models, improves convergence, improves trainability and provides a cost-function-level diagnostic for quantum phase transitions. Finally, we establish that a low cost value does not by itself guarantee convergence in trace distance. Nevertheless, it faithfully reproduces degeneracies and spectral gaps, which are essential for applications to topological phases.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes variational algorithms for learning entanglement Hamiltonians in quantum critical systems, improving convergence and reducing measurements.
motivation: Entanglement Hamiltonians are key to understanding quantum many-body systems, but their experimental extraction is challenging; variational methods offer a practical route.
method: The authors interpret the cost functional as an integral to deploy iterative quadrature schemes, and modify the ansatz to capture deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form.
result: The approach reduces required measurements by over an order of magnitude, improves convergence and trainability, and provides a diagnostic for quantum phase transitions.
conclusion: Low cost value does not guarantee convergence in trace distance, but the method faithfully reproduces degeneracies and spectral gaps relevant for topological phases.

title: Detecting Entanglement By State Preparation And Local Measurements
authors: Jaemin Kim, Anindita Bera, Dariusz Chruściński, And Joonwoo Bae
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2128 (2026).

Entanglement witnesses (EWs) are a collection of observables that can characterize separable states and, experimentally, estimating EWs can verify entangled states. In this work, we show that a fixed measurement setting on a multipartite entangled state, which we introduce as a network state for the purpose, can estimate EWs. Namely, entangled states can be fully verified in a measurement-based manner, in which experimenters do not necessarily change measurement settings. We present a fixed measurement setting and network states for estimating decomposable EWs, equivalent to the partial transpose criteria. We also consider non-decomposable EWs that detect bound entangled states beyond the partial transpose criteria. The results can be extended to multipartite states such as graph states, a resource for measurement-based quantum computing, and readily applied to distributed settings such as quantum metrology or sensor networks where multipartite entangled states are resourceful.

.
tldr: Proposes a fixed measurement setting and network states to estimate entanglement witnesses, enabling full verification of entangled states without changing measurement settings.
motivation: Entanglement witnesses are crucial for detecting entanglement, but standard methods require changing measurement settings; this work aims to simplify experimental verification.
method: Introduces a fixed measurement setting and network states that can estimate decomposable and non-decomposable entanglement witnesses, including those for bound entangled states and graph states.
result: Shows that entangled states can be fully verified in a measurement-based manner with a fixed setting, applicable to multipartite states and distributed settings.
conclusion: The approach provides a practical, resource-efficient method for entanglement detection, relevant to quantum metrology and sensor networks.

title: Exact Distinguishability Between Real-valued And Complex-valued Haar Random Quantum States
authors: Tristan Nemoz, Romain Alléaume, And Peter Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2120 (2026).

Haar random states are fundamental objects in quantum information theory and quantum computing. We study the density matrix resulting from sampling [MATH] copies of a [MATH]-dimensional quantum state according to the Haar measure on the orthogonal group. In particular, we analytically compute its spectral decomposition. This allows us to compute exactly the trace distance between [MATH]-copies of a real Haar random state and [MATH]-copies of a complex Haar random state. Using this we show a lower-bound on the approximation parameter of real-valued state [MATH]-designs and improve the lower-bound on the number of copies required for imaginarity testing.

.
tldr: This paper analytically computes the spectral decomposition of the density matrix of multiple copies of Haar random states from the orthogonal group, enabling exact distinguishability between real and complex Haar random states and improved bounds on real-valued state designs and imaginarity testing.
motivation: Understanding the distinguishability between real and complex random quantum states is fundamental for quantum information theory, state tomography, and the study of imaginarity as a resource.
method: The authors analytically compute the spectral decomposition of the density matrix resulting from sampling multiple copies of a Haar random state from the orthogonal group, using representation theory and Schur-Weyl duality.
result: They obtain exact expressions for the trace distance between copies of real and complex Haar random states, derive a lower bound on the approximation parameter of real-valued state t-designs, and improve the lower bound on the number of copies required for imaginarity testing.
conclusion: The work provides a complete analytical characterization of the distinguishability problem, with implications for quantum state designs and the resource theory of imaginarity.

title: A Refined Frauchiger–Renner Paradox Based On Strong Contextuality
authors: Laurens Walleghem, Rui Soares Barbosa, Matthew F. Pusey, And Stefan Weigert
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2116 (2026).

The Frauchiger–Renner paradox derives an inconsistency when quantum theory is used to describe the use of itself, by means of a scenario where agents model other agents quantumly and reason about each other's knowledge. We observe that logical contextuality (à la Hardy) is the key ingredient of the FR paradox, and we provide a stronger paradox based on the strongly contextual GHZ–Mermin scenario. In contrast to the FR paradox, this GHZ–FR paradox neither requires post-selection nor any reasoning by observers who are modelled quantumly. If one accepts the universality of quantum theory including superobservers, we propose a natural extension of Peres's dictum to resolve these extended Wigner's friend paradoxes.

.
tldr: The paper strengthens the Frauchiger–Renner paradox using strong contextuality from the GHZ–Mermin scenario, eliminating the need for post-selection or quantum self-reference.
motivation: To resolve inconsistencies in quantum theory when describing itself, and to clarify the role of contextuality in extended Wigner's friend scenarios.
method: The authors identify logical contextuality as the key ingredient of the original FR paradox and construct a stronger paradox based on the strongly contextual GHZ–Mermin scenario.
result: The GHZ–FR paradox is stronger than the original, requiring no post-selection or reasoning by agents modeled quantumly, and it highlights the foundational role of contextuality.
conclusion: The paradox suggests a natural extension of Peres's dictum to resolve extended Wigner's friend paradoxes, reinforcing the importance of contextuality in quantum foundations.

title: Optimal Control Of Engineered Swift Equilibration Of Nanomechanical Oscillators
authors: Julia Sanders And Paolo Muratore-Ginanneschi
abstract: Processes conveying physical information are always subject to speed limits. We explore the consequence of this in optimal control of indicators of finite-time thermodynamic transitions of nano-systems evolving according to an underdamped dynamics. Our main finding is that, in the presence of speed limits, problems like optimal engineered swift equilibration and transitions towards an out-of-equilibrium state at minimum work done to the system are well-posed. In particular, we show that there is no need for discontinuities in the internal energy at the end of the control horizon. This was a problem that raised doubts for a long time on the physical meaning of certain optimal transitions. We perform our analysis on the experimentally relevant case of nano-oscillators, and we expect our predictions on optimal protocols and the evolution of mean heat and work to be experimentally testable.
tldr: This paper studies optimal control of engineered swift equilibration for nanomechanical oscillators under speed limits, showing that discontinuities in internal energy are not required.
motivation: Speed limits constrain finite-time thermodynamic processes; the authors aim to resolve whether optimal protocols for swift equilibration require unphysical energy discontinuities.
method: They formulate optimal control problems for underdamped dynamics of nanomechanical oscillators, incorporating speed limits to find protocols that minimize work while achieving swift equilibration.
result: They prove that optimal protocols exist without internal energy discontinuities, and derive predictions for mean heat and work that are experimentally testable.
conclusion: The work establishes that optimal control of swift equilibration is well-posed under speed limits, providing practical protocols for nanoscale thermodynamic transitions.

title: Quantum Cryptography Beyond Key Distribution: Theory And Experiment
authors: Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, And Philip Walther
abstract:
Author(s): Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, and Philip Walther

Cryptography not only involves the sending of secret messages but also encompasses many protocols and procedures that provide privacy and security in the networked world. Likewise, quantum resources have the potential to enhance cryptography in ways that go beyond the well-known example of quantum key distribution. This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. It explains the security that they offer, including the sometimes significant limitations on their theoretical capabilities. Implementations using current photonic techniques are discussed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045006] Published Fri Dec 19, 2025.
tldr: A review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory and photonic implementations.
motivation: To classify and assess the security of quantum cryptographic protocols beyond key distribution, highlighting their potential and limitations.
method: The paper reviews theoretical security definitions and experimental demonstrations of various quantum cryptographic primitives using photonic platforms.
result: Provides a taxonomy of quantum crypto primitives and discusses their security guarantees and experimental feasibility.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers enhanced security for many tasks beyond QKD, but practical implementations face significant challenges.

title: Tuning Ergodicity Breaking: Anomalous Diffusion Under Asymptotic Power-law Forcing
authors: Raul V. B. Mor\'as (instituto Latino-Americano de Ci\^encias Da Vida E Da Natureza, Universidade Federal Da Integra\c{c}\~ao Latino-Americana, 85867-970 Foz Do Igua\c{c}u, Paran\'a, Brazil), M. Florencia Carusela (instituto de Ciencias, Universidad Nacional de General Sarmiento, Los Polvorines, Buenos Aires, Argentina, National Scientific And Technical Research Council, Argentina), Luciano C. Lapas
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20807v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In non-Markovian systems, distinct dynamical phases arise from the competition between internal memory and external forcing, encompassing thermalization, persistent ergodicity breaking, and runaway energy growth. This study shows that the scaling parameter [MATH] governs the emergent phase diagram within a system described by the Generalized Langevin Equation, particularly when subjected to external drives with asymptotic power-law tails. Three universal regimes for diffusive processes are delineated by this parameter: thermalization ([MATH]), non-ergodic saturation ([MATH]), and a force-dominated runaway phase ([MATH]). The fluctuation-dissipation theorem, within this framework, is shown to be independent of external force and determined by the integral of noise density of states. A selective breaking of ergodicity is revealed by this formulation; microscopic fluctuations are decoupled from the drive, yet the relaxation completely encodes it, which in turn controls the kinetic effective temperature. Direct Langevin simulations in the Markovian limit quantitatively confirm this classification, capturing the non-thermal plateau at the critical point.
tldr: This paper studies ergodicity breaking and anomalous diffusion in non-Markovian systems under asymptotic power-law forcing, identifying three universal dynamical regimes.
motivation: Understanding the interplay between memory effects and external driving in non-Markovian systems is crucial for characterizing non-equilibrium dynamics and ergodicity breaking.
method: The authors analyze a Generalized Langevin Equation with power-law correlated noise and external drives, deriving a scaling parameter that governs the phase diagram. Direct Langevin simulations in the Markovian limit confirm the classification.
result: Three regimes are identified: thermalization, non-ergodic saturation, and a force-dominated runaway phase. The fluctuation-dissipation theorem is shown to be independent of external force, and a selective breaking of ergodicity is revealed.
conclusion: The scaling parameter provides a universal classification of diffusive regimes in non-Markovian systems, with implications for understanding ergodicity breaking and effective temperature in driven systems.

title: Enhancing Quantum Processor Capabilities During Idle Times

abstract: ArXiv:2606.20841v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We advocate an alternative paradigm to operate quantum computers that utilizes multipartite entanglement generated in dedicated auxiliary systems during idle times. This stored entanglement enhances the future capabilities of the quantum processor, as it can be flexibly used to assist and speed-up computations when needed. We identify classes of multipartite entangled resource states whose computational power are related to their entanglement features, and in turn to the complexity to generate them. During idle times, one can thus continuously work towards generating more and more powerful auxiliary multipartite entangled states. Idle times include both times prior to the start of a computation, but also any step during the execution of an algorithm where parts of the processor are not actively involved. To illustrate our approach, we consider architectures with limited connectivity, e.g. corresponding to a 1D geometry. We show that [MATH]-dimensional cluster states allow one to flexibly perform multiple long-distance two-qubit gates in parallel, where both the complexity to generate them, as well as the number of achievable gates increases with [MATH].

title: Hydrodynamic Tails In Chaotic Spin Chains With Quantum Group Symmetry
authors: Luca V. Delacretaz, Victor Gorbenko, Jiaozi Wang, Bernardo Zan, Aleksandr Zhabin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The interplay between symmetry and thermalization governs the late-time dynamics of local quantum and classical many-body systems at nonzero temperature. Recently, two parallel frontiers have emerged: the search for robust anomalous hydrodynamics -- such as superdiffusion -- in generic, non-integrable models, and the formal effort to generalize the fundamental concept of global symmetry. In this paper, we bridge these frontiers by demonstrating that quantum group symmetry provides a novel mechanism for anomalous hydrodynamics in chaotic systems. We study the dynamics of local operators carrying [MATH] charge in non-integrable lattice models that also have quantum group symmetry. One example is transverse spin in the XXZ model with integrability breaking deformations. While such excitations are expected to decay very quickly at high temperature because their charge forbids overlap with conventional hydrodynamic densities, we find that protection by the quantum group symmetry makes these modes long-lived, despite the absence of local quantum group charge density or current. Furthermore, the dynamics is superdiffusive across Hamiltonian, Floquet, and classical realizations, and exhibits unusual finite size effects at very late times. We also revisit transverse spin dynamics in the integrable XXZ model.

motivation: To understand how generalized symmetries can produce anomalous hydrodynamics (superdiffusion) in non-integrable many-body systems, bridging symmetry and thermalization.
method: Study non-integrable lattice models (e.g., XXZ with integrability-breaking deformations) that possess quantum group symmetry; analyze dynamics of local operators carrying quantum group charge via numerical and analytical techniques.
result: Operators protected by quantum group symmetry exhibit long-lived, superdiffusive dynamics across Hamiltonian, Floquet, and classical realizations, with unusual finite-size effects.
conclusion: Quantum group symmetry provides a robust mechanism for anomalous hydrodynamics in chaotic systems, offering a new route to superdiffusion beyond integrability.

title: Hierarchical Separation Of Relaxation Timescales From Spectral Localization Bounds
authors: Alex Stewart-Bozzo, Jakub Garwo{\l}a, Brett Min, Dvira Segal
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the dissipative dynamics of multilevel quantum systems strongly coupled either to a lossy cavity mode or directly to a bosonic environment. By deriving spectral localization bounds, we establish conditions under which strong system-bath coupling gives rise to a hierarchy of population relaxation timescales. Our approach builds on the reaction-coordinate polaron-transform framework. By mapping the original strong-coupling problem onto an effective weakly dissipative model, we analyze the spectrum of the resulting Liouvillian superoperator through localization bounds. For the generalized V model, we find that strong system-bath coupling gives rise to a bright-dark structure in the effective system-bath coupling operator: a single collective mode remains strongly coupled to the environment, while the remaining modes become progressively dark. Consequently, the dynamics separate into fast and slow sectors and, at finite coupling strengths, develop a hierarchy of population relaxation timescales. Numerical simulations based on both secular and non-secular quantum master equations corroborate the emergence of timescale separation and the pronounced slowing down of dissipative dynamics at strong coupling. Our results reveal a general mechanism underlying anomalously slow relaxation in strongly coupled open quantum systems and provide a route for engineering long-lived states through system-environment interactions.

method: The authors use the reaction-coordinate polaron-transform framework to map the strong-coupling problem onto an effective weakly dissipative model, then analyze the Liouvillian spectrum via localization bounds.
result: They show that strong system-bath coupling creates a bright-dark structure in the coupling operator, leading to a hierarchy of relaxation timescales with fast and slow sectors.
conclusion: The results reveal a general mechanism for slow relaxation and provide a way to engineer long-lived states via system-environment interactions.

title: Finite-Time Electrometry With A Quantum-Regime Single-Ion Phonon Laser
authors: Pei-Dong Li, Yuan-Zhang Dong, Zhuo-Zhu Wu, Jia-Wei Wang, Ji Li, Jian-Qi Zhang, Zhi-Jiao Deng, Liang Chen, Mang Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.21068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The phonon laser realized in a trapped ion, i.e., a self-sustained mechanical oscillator, has demonstrated the unique characteristics in practically detecting externally applied electric signals without the prerequisite of sideband cooling. Entering the quantum regime via sideband cooling is expected to further improve its sensing performance. Here we report the first experimental realization of a quantum-regime single-ion phonon laser ([MATH]) using a trapped [MATH] ion and demonstrate electrometry based on its phase-space symmetry-breaking response to weak resonant electric fields. By tuning the phonon-laser parameters, we reveal that the sensing performance is fundamentally governed by the finite-time relaxation dynamics of the underlying open quantum system. We find that a slow Liouvillian relaxation, correlated with the finite experimental interaction window, effectively enhances the dynamic susceptibility while maintaining the structural robustness of the limit cycle. This regime, when applied to the detection of electric fields, produces a shot-noise-limited peak sensitivity of [MATH] and a minimum detectable field variation of [MATH]. Our results establish quantum phonon lasers as a practical platform for advanced sensing and highlight the central role of Liouvillian dynamics in non-equilibrium electrometry.

method: Trapped 40Ca+ ion is sideband-cooled to the quantum regime to realize a phonon laser; weak resonant electric fields are applied and the phase-space symmetry-breaking response is measured.

title: Reducing Measurement Error With Adaptivity
authors: James Byrne, Noah Linden, Paul Skrzypczyk
abstract: ArXiv:2606.21283v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that adaptivity, also called feed-forward, is a powerful resource in reducing the error of measurement circuits that combine multiple uses of a noisy measuring device. In previous work, it has been shown that error in measurements can be mitigated by using the measuring device multiple times. So far, the most effective protocols have been parallel measurement schemes, where all measurements are simultaneous. We extend this idea to adaptive measurement schemes, where the results of previous measurements can influence our choice of processing further down the circuit. We show that adaptive measurement circuits can in general reduce overall measurement errors further than any non-adaptive measurement circuit could with the same number of measurements. In particular, we show that for a large class of noisy two-outcome qubit measurements, such an adaptive advantage can exist when as few as three measurements are used. We also show that the adaptive advantage is unbounded across the class of noisy two-outcome qubit measurements, as the number of uses of the device increases. As part of this work, we devise and use methods for finding optimal measurement circuits in both the non-adaptive and adaptive cases. In addition, we prove general results about the limits of such circuits, both in measuring a qubit, and more generally, a qudit.
tldr: Adaptive measurement circuits can reduce measurement error beyond non-adaptive protocols for noisy qubit measurements.
motivation: Measurement errors limit quantum information processing; using a noisy device multiple times can mitigate errors, but previous work focused on parallel schemes.
method: The authors develop methods to find optimal adaptive and non-adaptive measurement circuits, analyzing a class of noisy two-outcome qubit measurements.
result: Adaptive circuits outperform non-adaptive ones for as few as three measurements, and the advantage is unbounded as the number of measurements increases.
conclusion: Adaptivity is a powerful resource for error reduction in quantum measurements, with implications for quantum information processing and metrology.
