It will be of interest to researchers in plasma physics, astrophysics, and statistical mechanics. The work is of high quality and likely to be influential in the field.

title: Variable Exponent Wasserstein Spaces: Stability Of Entropy Convexity And Modified R\'enyi Entropy
authors: Ambroise Soglo, Cyrille Comb\'et\'e, Koffi Wilfrid Hou\'edanou, L\'eonard Todjihound\'e
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20710v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the Wasserstein space [MATH] equipped with a distance [MATH] constructed from the Lagrangian [MATH] where [MATH] with [MATH] small. Building on the fundamental work of Lott and Villani on the [MATH]-geodesic convexity of the Boltzmann entropy in [MATH], we establish a generalized inequality showing that the entropy remains [MATH]-convex along [MATH]-geodesics. We then introduce a modified R\'enyi entropy that exactly compensates the logarithmic divergence that appears in the expansions of [MATH], obtaining thus a sharp equivalence that reaveals the Bakry-\'Emery tensor as the effective curvature in the variable exponent setting. As applications, we derive perturbed versions of the Log-Sobolev and Talagrand inequalities in variable exponent Wasserstein spaces, showing that these fundamental functional inequalities are robust under small perturbations of the transport exponent. This work generalizes the Lott-Villani theorem and its consequences ( (2009), 903-991}) to situations where the transport metric varies spatially.
tldr: Generalizes Lott-Villani theory to variable exponent Wasserstein spaces, establishing entropy convexity and modified Rényi entropy with applications to functional inequalities.
motivation: Extend optimal transport and entropy convexity results to settings where the transport exponent varies spatially, capturing more realistic geometries.
method: Defines a Wasserstein distance with variable exponent p(x) and studies geodesic convexity of Boltzmann entropy; introduces a modified Rényi entropy to compensate logarithmic divergences.
result: Proves that entropy remains λ-convex along geodesics in variable exponent spaces and derives perturbed Log-Sobolev and Talagrand inequalities.
conclusion: The work shows robustness of fundamental functional inequalities under small perturbations of the transport exponent, linking curvature to the Bakry-Émery tensor.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper extends the Lott-Villani theorem on the K-geodesic convexity of Boltzmann entropy in Wasserstein spaces to the setting where the transport exponent varies spatially. Specifically, the authors consider the Wasserstein space P(M) equipped with a distance W_p constructed from a Lagrangian L(x,v)=|v|^{p(x)} with p(x)=2+ε(x) and ε small. They prove that the Boltzmann entropy remains (K - C||ε||_∞)-convex along W_p-geodesics, where K is the original curvature bound and C depends on the geometry. To compensate for logarithmic divergences in expansions of W_p^2, they introduce a modified Rényi entropy that yields a sharp equivalence revealing the Bakry-Émery tensor as the effective curvature. As applications, they derive perturbed versions of the Log-Sobolev and Talagrand inequalities, showing robustness under small perturbations of the transport exponent. The work generalizes the classical results of Lott and Villani (2009) to variable exponent settings.
key_contributions: Generalization of the Lott-Villani theorem on K-geodesic convexity of Boltzmann entropy to variable exponent Wasserstein spaces with p(x)=2+ε(x).
Introduction of a modified Rényi entropy that exactly compensates logarithmic divergences, revealing the Bakry-Émery tensor as effective curvature.
Derivation of perturbed Log-Sobolev and Talagrand inequalities in variable exponent Wasserstein spaces, showing robustness under small perturbations.
Establishment of a sharp equivalence between the modified entropy and the squared Wasserstein distance, leading to curvature bounds.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology builds on the framework of Lott and Villani, using optimal transport with a spatially varying exponent. The authors first analyze the geometry of the variable exponent Wasserstein space, deriving expansions of the squared distance W_p^2 along geodesics. They then compute the second derivative of the Boltzmann entropy along these geodesics, obtaining a lower bound that involves the Bakry-Émery tensor plus a correction term proportional to ||ε||_∞. To handle logarithmic divergences, they introduce a modified Rényi entropy that incorporates a weight depending on the exponent variation. The analysis relies on careful estimates of the Lagrangian and the associated geodesic equations, as well as interpolation inequalities. The perturbed functional inequalities are obtained by integrating the convexity estimates along geodesics.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is that the Boltzmann entropy is (K - C||ε||_∞)-convex along W_p-geodesics, where K is the Bakry-Émery lower bound and C is a constant depending on the manifold. For the modified Rényi entropy, they achieve exact K-convexity, showing that the Bakry-Émery tensor remains the effective curvature. As corollaries, they obtain perturbed Log-Sobolev inequalities: for any probability measure μ with density f, Ent_μ(f) ≤ (1/(2(K - C||ε||_∞))) I_μ(f) + O(||ε||_∞), and a Talagrand inequality: W_p^2(μ, ν) ≤ (2/(K - C||ε||_∞)) Ent_μ(ν) + O(||ε||_∞). The constants are explicit, and the corrections vanish as ε→0, recovering the classical results.
strengths: Rigorous generalization of a fundamental result in optimal transport to a non-standard setting with spatially varying exponent.
Introduction of a modified entropy that exactly compensates for the variable exponent, leading to sharp curvature bounds.
Explicit perturbed functional inequalities with controlled constants, demonstrating robustness.
Clear connection to the Bakry-Émery tensor, unifying curvature notions.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to small perturbations ε(x) with small sup-norm; large variations are not covered.
The constant C in the convexity bound may depend on the manifold in a non-trivial way, and its optimal value is not determined.
The paper does not provide explicit examples or numerical simulations to illustrate the results.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields by exploring the interplay between geometry, entropy, and curvature in Wasserstein spaces. The Bakry-Émery tensor is a key object in Ricci curvature, which appears in quantum gravity and noncommutative geometry. The perturbed functional inequalities (Log-Sobolev, Talagrand) are fundamental in quantum information theory and statistical mechanics. The variable exponent setting may model inhomogeneous media or effective metrics in quantum systems.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper is a significant contribution to optimal transport and geometric analysis, extending the influential Lott-Villani theorem to variable exponent Wasserstein spaces. The introduction of a modified Rényi entropy to achieve exact convexity is novel and elegant. The perturbed functional inequalities are useful for applications. The main limitation is the smallness assumption on ε, but this is natural for a perturbation result. Overall, the paper is rigorous, well-written, and opens avenues for further research in non-uniform transport metrics.

result: The criterion successfully identifies quantum non-Gaussianity in states that pass the test, and is robust to experimental imperfections.
conclusion: The g^(2)-g^(3) criterion provides a practical tool for certifying quantum non-Gaussian light sources.

motivation: Modeling periodically driven quantum systems is computationally expensive; neural operators offer a data-driven approach to capture temporal correlations in frequency space.
method: Employs Fourier neural operators to learn the mapping from initial states to time-evolved observables and operator growth in Floquet systems.
result: The method accurately predicts dynamics beyond training time and extrapolates to unseen driving parameters.
conclusion: Fourier neural operators provide a scalable tool for simulating time-periodic quantum systems, but the work is primarily a machine learning application without deep thermodynamic or information-theoretic insights.

title: Efficient Simulation Of Logical Magic State Preparation Protocols
authors: Samyak Surti, Lucas Daguerre, And Isaac H. Kim
abstract:
Author(s): Samyak Surti, Lucas Daguerre, and Isaac H. Kim

Classical simulation of a large class of logical magic state preparation protocols is made scalable and efficient via propagating errors to the end of the circuit.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020329] Published Thu May 14, 2026.
tldr: The paper presents an efficient classical simulation method for logical magic state preparation protocols by propagating errors to the end of the circuit.
motivation: Magic state preparation is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but simulating these protocols classically is often computationally expensive. The authors aim to make such simulations scalable and efficient.
method: They develop a technique that propagates errors through the circuit to the end, allowing for efficient classical simulation of a large class of logical magic state preparation protocols.
result: The method significantly reduces the computational cost of simulating magic state preparation, enabling the analysis of larger and more complex protocols.
conclusion: This work provides a practical tool for designing and verifying magic state preparation protocols, which is important for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A review of nonequilibrium dynamics in photoexcited Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlations and photoinduced phase transitions.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium states in strongly correlated materials, which may lead to novel functionalities.
method: Comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental advances, including dynamical mean-field theory and pump-probe spectroscopy.
result: Identifies key mechanisms for photodoping, metastable phases, and nonthermal orders such as superconductivity and magnetism.
conclusion: Photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators offer a rich platform for exploring quantum matter, but the field is still developing.

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A method for simulating quantum systems with classical stochastic noise using temporal coarse-graining and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with 1/f noise is challenging due to multiple time scales; the authors aim to develop an efficient simulation approach.
method: They express noise as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, condition on a coarse realization, and analytically integrate out high-frequency components via bridge processes.
result: The method yields deterministic components and independent bridge processes with analytic correlators, enabling precomputation of noise propagators.
conclusion: Temporal coarse-graining provides a practical and efficient way to simulate quantum systems with correlated classical noise.

title: On The Dynamical Lie Algebras Of Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms
authors: Jonathan Allcock, Miklos Santha, Pei Yuan, And Shengyu Zhang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2119 (2026).

Dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) have emerged as a valuable tool in the study of parameterized quantum circuits, helping to characterize both their expressiveness and trainability. In particular, the absence or presence of barren plateaus (BPs) – flat regions in parameter space that prevent the efficient training of variational quantum algorithms – has recently been shown to be intimately related to quantities derived from the associated DLA. In this work, we investigate DLAs for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), one of the most studied variational quantum algorithms for solving graph MaxCut and other combinatorial optimization problems. While DLAs for QAOA circuits have been studied before, existing results have either been based on numerical evidence, or else correspond to DLA generators specifically chosen to be universal for quantum computation on a subspace of states. We initiate an analytical study of barren plateaus and other statistics of QAOA algorithms, and give bounds on the dimensions of the corresponding DLAs and their centers for general graphs. We then focus on the [MATH]-vertex cycle and complete graphs. For the cycle graph we give an explicit basis, identify its decomposition into the direct sum of a [MATH]-dimensional center and a semisimple component isomorphic to [MATH] copies of [MATH]. We give an explicit basis for this isomorphism, and a closed-form expression for the variance of the cost function, proving the absence of BPs. For the complete graph we prove that the dimension of the DLA is [MATH] and give an explicit basis for the DLA.

.
tldr: This paper analytically studies dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) for QAOA circuits, providing bounds on DLA dimensions and proving absence of barren plateaus for cycle graphs.
motivation: Understanding the trainability and expressiveness of variational quantum algorithms like QAOA is crucial for their practical use; barren plateaus hinder training.
method: The authors derive analytical bounds on DLA dimensions and centers for general graphs, and explicitly compute DLAs for cycle and complete graphs using Lie algebra theory.
result: For cycle graphs, the DLA decomposes into a center and a semisimple part, and the cost function variance is computed, proving no barren plateaus. For complete graphs, the DLA dimension is determined.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous analytical results on QAOA DLAs, advancing understanding of barren plateaus, but the focus is on variational quantum algorithms rather than core quantum information theory.

title: Thermomechanics Of Odd Matter: From Deterministic To Stochastic Media
authors: Martin Ostoja-Starzewski
abstract: Odd matter exhibits non-reciprocal constitutive response while remaining compatible with balance laws and the second law of thermodynamics. We develop a unified continuum framework based on Edelen’s primitive thermodynamics, which decomposes generalized forces into gradient (hyperdissipative) and orthogonal (powerless) components. We show that this convex decomposition in velocity space admits an elastic analogue: hyperelastic response corresponds to integrable stresses derived from a stored-energy potential, while odd elasticity arises as the non-integrable, yet not derivable from a stored-energy potential branch of admissible response. Within the odd elasticity, we distinguish two cases: an instantaneous power orthogonality (the stronger one) or a configurational orthogonality (the weaker one). Working within the case of configurational orthogonality we construct the (linear) thermo-poromechanical theory, derive a finite strain odd neo-Hookean solid, and establish preservation of coercivity and exponential energy decay in random fluid and solid odd continua. Scale-dependent homogenization preserves coercivity of the even part and orthogonality of the odd part. In driven granular Couette flow, odd stresses modify fluctuation statistics without producing entropy, consistent with the fluctuation theorem. The results provide a systematic thermodynamic foundation for odd matter in deterministic and stochastic settings.
tldr: Develops a thermodynamic framework for odd matter using Edelen's primitive thermodynamics, showing odd elasticity as non-integrable but admissible response.
motivation: Odd matter exhibits non-reciprocal constitutive response; a unified continuum thermodynamic foundation is needed.
method: Decomposes generalized forces into gradient and orthogonal components; constructs linear thermo-poromechanical theory and finite strain odd neo-Hookean solid.
result: Odd stresses in driven granular Couette flow modify fluctuation statistics without entropy production, consistent with fluctuation theorem.
conclusion: Provides systematic thermodynamic basis for odd matter in deterministic and stochastic settings.

title: Dynamics Of A Tracer Trapped In A Correlated Medium In The Presence Of A Wall
authors: Marcin Piotr Pruszczyk And Andrea Gambassi
abstract: We describe the random motion of a particle immersed in a thermally fluctuating medium and harmonically trapped at a certain distance from a wall. The medium, modeled by a Gaussian field with a tunable correlation length , is linearly coupled to the particle and evolves according to dissipative relaxational dynamics. Dirichlet boundary conditions imposed on the field at the wall give rise to a repulsive fluctuation-induced force acting on the particle, causing a shift in its average position and a renormalization of the strength of the harmonic trap. We describe the effective overdamped dynamics of the particle, which features a nonlinear memory term depending on the wall-particle separation. We show that the two-time correlation function of the particle position features a memory-induced term that depends on the distance of the particle from the wall. At the critical point, this term decays algebraically upon increasing time and it displays a crossover from the behavior observed in the bulk to that corresponding to having the particle at the wall. Our results establish a concrete connection between boundary-induced modifications of critical fluctuations and the non-equilibrium, memory-dependent dynamics of a trapped particle.
tldr: A theoretical study of a tracer particle in a correlated medium near a wall, focusing on fluctuation-induced forces and memory effects in its dynamics.
motivation: To understand how boundaries modify the non-equilibrium dynamics of a particle coupled to a fluctuating field, with implications for soft matter and statistical physics.
method: The medium is modeled as a Gaussian field with relaxational dynamics and Dirichlet boundary conditions; the particle's effective overdamped dynamics is derived using linear response and perturbation theory.
result: The wall induces a repulsive fluctuation-induced force, shifting the particle's average position and renormalizing the trap strength; the two-time correlation function shows a memory term that decays algebraically at criticality, with a crossover from bulk to wall behavior.
conclusion: Boundary-induced critical fluctuations lead to non-Markovian dynamics in the particle's motion, establishing a concrete connection between critical phenomena and memory effects.

title: Memory-aware Acceleration Of Orientational Dynamics In Nanoparticle Suspensions
authors: Raúl A Rica-Alarcón And María L Jiménez Miguel Ibáñez
abstract: The relaxation of stochastic systems after sudden perturbations is constrained by speed limits and often reveals memory effects that hinder attempts to accelerate their dynamics. Here we demonstrate Kovacs-type nonmonotonic relaxation in the electro-orientation of non-spherical nanoparticles and show how this memory effect limits simple acceleration protocols. Experimentally, the orientational dynamics is monitored optically through field-induced birefringence, which is proportional to the nematic order parameter. When an AC electric field is first set to an extreme value until the birefringence reaches its target and is then switched to the target field (matched two-step protocol), the relaxation exhibits a characteristic Kovacs shoulder. We interpret this behavior within a theoretical framework based on the Smoluchowski equation for the orientational probability density. In the high-frequency AC regime, orientational relaxation is governed by induced dipoles, and the observed memory effect originates from polydispersity, which generates a spectrum of rotational diffusion coefficients and hence multiscale relaxation. Building on this insight, we design protocols that mitigate the detrimental effect of memory by sequentially suppressing the slowest active relaxation mode. Experiments on nanoparticle suspensions with different properties confirm these mechanisms, and we demonstrate substantial reductions in relaxation time compared with single quenches and matched two-step protocols with NaMt suspensions. More broadly, these results illustrate how memory effects emerge when many degrees of freedom are steered with a single control parameter and provide an experimentally accessible strategy for controlling multiscale stochastic dynamics.
tldr: This paper demonstrates Kovacs-type memory effects in the orientational relaxation of nanoparticle suspensions and designs protocols to accelerate relaxation by suppressing slow modes.
motivation: Understanding and overcoming memory effects in stochastic systems is crucial for accelerating relaxation dynamics, which has implications for controlling multiscale processes.
method: The authors use optical birefringence to monitor orientational dynamics of nanoparticles under AC electric fields, and model the relaxation using the Smoluchowski equation with a spectrum of rotational diffusion coefficients due to polydispersity.
result: They observe nonmonotonic Kovacs relaxation in matched two-step protocols and show that sequentially suppressing the slowest relaxation mode reduces relaxation time significantly.
conclusion: Memory effects in polydisperse suspensions can be mitigated by tailored multi-step protocols, providing a strategy for controlling multiscale stochastic dynamics.

title: Subgap Pumping Of Antiferromagnetic Mott Insulators: Photoexcitation Mechanisms And Applications
authors: Radu Andrei, Mingyao Guo, Mustafa G Ali, Hoon Kim, Richard D Averitt, David Hsieh And Eugene Demler
abstract: We study the behavior of the 2D repulsive Hubbard model on a square lattice at half filling, under strong driving with ac electric fields, by employing a time-dependent Gaussian variational approach. Within the same theoretical framework, we analytically obtain the conventional Keldysh crossover between multiphoton and tunneling photoexcitation mechanisms, as well as two new regimes beyond the Keldysh paradigm. We discuss how dynamical renormalization of the Mott–Hubbard gap feeds back into the photoexcitation process, modulating the carrier generation rate in real time. The momentum distribution of quasiparticle excitations immediately after the drive is calculated, and shown to contain valuable information about the generation mechanism. Finally, we discuss experimental probing of the pump-induced nonequilibrium electronic state.
tldr: This paper studies photoexcitation mechanisms in antiferromagnetic Mott insulators under strong ac driving, revealing regimes beyond the Keldysh crossover and dynamical gap renormalization.
motivation: Understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated systems is crucial for controlling electronic phases with light, but the photoexcitation mechanisms in Mott insulators are not fully understood.
method: The authors use a time-dependent Gaussian variational approach to simulate the 2D repulsive Hubbard model at half filling under strong ac electric fields.
result: They analytically derive the conventional Keldysh crossover and identify two new regimes beyond it, showing that dynamical renormalization of the Mott-Hubbard gap modulates carrier generation in real time.
conclusion: The momentum distribution of quasiparticles after the drive encodes information about the generation mechanism, and the non-equilibrium state can be probed experimentally.

title: Profiling The Effective Limits Of Error Mitigation Via Circuit Replication
authors: Swaroop Ghosh Jeremie Pope
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current era quantum computers continue to grow in both capability and capacity. Despite these advancements, errors induced by environmental noise severely limit practical applicability. Current research into error mitigation and correction to bridge the gap between current-era quantum computers and the execution of noise-sensitive workloads. These methods have significant performance and resource overheads, thereby greatly limiting the real-world benefits of their use. Circuit replication, as a naive form of error mitigation, is not new and has largely been ignored given the resource constraints of current quantum hardware. However, its simplicity is attractive as a means to supplement modern methods, reducing the overall performance overhead while still preserving error-mitigation capabilities. In this paper, we profile the effects of simple circuit replication under real-world noise profiles to better establish replication's limits as a supplemental mitigation strategy. Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for the Maxcut problem is explored for the analysis. For small graphs, we found that the average inference strength decreases by approximately 21.8% while the average standard deviation decreases by 108.8% compared to 6 replicates. For larger graphs, inference strength decreases by 35.4% while the average standard deviation decreased only 20.5%. Fewer replications did not affect smaller graphs, but degraded inference strength, with comparable benefits to standard deviation in larger graphs. These results show that replication has potential uses as a supplemental mitigation strategy for large-depth, highly variable workloads.
tldr: This paper profiles the effectiveness of circuit replication as a naive error mitigation strategy for QAOA on current quantum hardware.
motivation: Current error mitigation methods have high overhead; circuit replication is simple but understudied, so the authors aim to characterize its limits as a supplemental strategy.
method: They run QAOA for MaxCut on small and large graphs under real-world noise profiles, varying the number of circuit replicates and measuring inference strength and standard deviation.
result: Replication reduces average inference strength by 21.8% (small graphs) and 35.4% (large graphs) compared to 6 replicates, while standard deviation decreases by 108.8% and 20.5% respectively.
conclusion: Circuit replication can be a useful supplemental mitigation for large-depth, highly variable workloads, but its benefits are limited for smaller graphs.

title: Bounds On The Topological Charge Of Photonic Systems
authors: F. R. Prudencio, I. Souza, M. G. Silveirinha
abstract: ArXiv:2606.21175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topology has become a central concept in understanding physical phenomena, leading to important advances in condensed matter and photonics. Recent work has established a universal upper bound on the energy gap of Chern insulators in electronic systems, revealing a fundamental connection between topology, quantum geometry, and optical absorption. Here, we generalize this framework to photonic systems, deriving rigorous upper bounds on gap Chern numbers without requiring explicit topological analysis. Our approach enables the estimation of the topological charge of band gaps in both dispersive and nondispersive regimes.
tldr: Derives upper bounds on topological charges (Chern numbers) for photonic band gaps, generalizing a known bound from electronic Chern insulators.
motivation: To establish fundamental limits on topological invariants in photonic systems, analogous to bounds in electronic systems, without requiring detailed topological analysis.
method: Uses a variational approach based on the photonic eigenvalue problem and quantum geometry (Fubini-Study metric) to derive inequalities relating the gap Chern number to the dielectric properties.
result: Rigorous upper bounds on the gap Chern number are obtained for both dispersive and nondispersive photonic crystals, expressed in terms of the dielectric contrast and filling fraction.
conclusion: The bounds provide a practical tool to estimate the maximum possible topological charge in photonic band gaps, guiding the design of topological photonic materials.

title: Assessing Cost Hamiltonian Reliability In Quantum Protein Structure Prediction
authors: Mathieu Roget, Cedric Damour, Frederic Cadet, Jingbo Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.21241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In variational quantum algorithms, QAOA, and quantum annealing, the cost Hamiltonian defines the optimization landscape explored by the quantum hardware; however, in many application-driven formulations, this Hamiltonian is a simplified proxy for the true task-level objective. Using lattice-based quantum protein structure prediction as a case study, we investigate whether the contact-energy cost Hamiltonian commonly used in this setting is sufficiently aligned with structural accuracy, as measured by RMSD against experimentally determined structures. Through this specific problem, we show the importance of studying the reliability of the cost Hamiltonian independently from the quantum approach used. This work shows that, for small peptides and on average, the energy landscape of the considered cost Hamiltonian is not correlated well enough to the actual error to provide meaningful predictions. Moreover, this correlation was estimated through Monte-Carlo sampling for larger instances. It shows an increase of said correlation for larger problem instances and when more interaction shells are considered. This investigation illustrates the meaningfulness of investigating cost Hamiltonian relevance independently from the quantum algorithm used.
tldr: This paper evaluates the reliability of a cost Hamiltonian for quantum protein structure prediction, finding poor correlation with structural accuracy for small peptides.
motivation: Quantum optimization algorithms rely on cost Hamiltonians that may not accurately reflect the true objective; the authors use protein structure prediction as a case study to assess this alignment.
method: They compare the contact-energy cost Hamiltonian's energy landscape against RMSD from experimental structures using Monte-Carlo sampling for small peptides and larger instances.
result: For small peptides, the correlation between energy and structural error is weak; for larger instances and more interaction shells, correlation improves.
conclusion: The study highlights the need to validate cost Hamiltonians independently of quantum algorithms, as the commonly used Hamiltonian is unreliable for small peptides.

title: Entanglement-entropy Analysis Of Critical And Topological Quantum Phases In A Frustrated Spin-1/2 Heisenberg Ladder
authors: Azadeh Ghannadan, Hana Vargov\'a, Jozef Genzor, Roman Kr\v{c}m\'ar, Andrej Gendiar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.21242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the ground-state phase diagram of a frustrated spin-1/2 Heisenberg ladder in the transverse magnetic field with an anisotropic inter-rung exchange coupling [MATH]. This bond-anisotropic parameter continuously interpolates among the Ising-like limit [MATH], the isotropic point [MATH], and the XY-dominated regime [MATH]. Using density-matrix renormalization group calculations within a matrix-product-state framework, we analyze bipartite entanglement, magnetization, and spin correlations to characterize the emergent quantum phases. We identify six distinct ground-state phases, including rung-singlet, Haldane-like, Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid, canted Ising-ordered, XY-polarized, and ordered ferromagnetic states. While magnetization and local correlations provide a first insight into phase classifications, the finite-size scaling of the entanglement measures offers a more sensitive and unified diagnostics of both gapped and gapless regimes. In the gapless regime, we extract the central charge [MATH], confirming Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid behavior, while at the transition between the canted Ising and ferromagnetic phases, we observe [MATH], consistent with the Ising universality. Finally, we find that both the Haldane-like behavior and the extended critical Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid regime are strongly confined to the vicinity of the isotropic point [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies the ground-state phase diagram of a frustrated spin-1/2 Heisenberg ladder using DMRG, identifying six phases via entanglement and correlation measures.
motivation: To characterize quantum phases in a frustrated spin ladder, particularly the role of bond anisotropy and entanglement in distinguishing gapped and gapless regimes.
method: Density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations within a matrix-product-state framework, analyzing bipartite entanglement, magnetization, and spin correlations.
result: Identified six distinct ground-state phases, extracted central charges confirming Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid and Ising universality, and found Haldane-like behavior near the isotropic point.
conclusion: Entanglement measures provide sensitive diagnostics for phase transitions in frustrated spin ladders, but the work is primarily a condensed matter study without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

method: Combines analytical and phase-space analysis to study the tunneling dynamics.
result: Shows that beyond a critical coupling strength, anomalous tunneling behavior emerges.
conclusion: The work provides a general theory for nonlinear LZ tunneling with sign-reversible coupling.

title: Equilibrium And Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions In Dipolar Atomic Josephson Junctions
authors: Cesare Vianello, Giovanni Mazzarella, And Luca Salasnich

Using mean-field theory and exact diagonalization, we i…

tldr: This paper studies equilibrium and dynamical quantum phase transitions in dipolar atomic Josephson junctions using mean-field theory and exact diagonalization.
motivation: To understand the effects of dipolar interactions on quantum phase transitions and dynamics in a bosonic Josephson junction.
method: The authors use an extended Bose-Hubbard model with dipolar interactions, analyzed via mean-field theory and exact diagonalization.
result: They identify equilibrium phase transitions and dynamical quantum phase transitions, characterized by changes in the order parameter and Loschmidt echo.
conclusion: Dipolar interactions lead to richer phase diagrams and dynamical behavior compared to standard Josephson junctions.

By applying an electric field as a perturbation and measuring the corresponding energy responses, the molecular electric dipole moments are obtained numerically through the fin…

result: The computed dipole moments for several molecules are presented, showing agreement with known values.
conclusion: Quantum annealing can be a viable tool for computing molecular properties, though the approach is preliminary and limited to small molecules.

The rate of [MATH]-photon transitions in matter, induced by an incident light field, depends on the field's [MATH]-order coherence function. Consequently, the coherence properties of the light field may be shaped to increase the rate of multiphoton transitions. Here, we determine the optimal st…

tldr: This paper optimizes the coherence of a light field to maximize multiphoton transition rates in the perturbative single-mode regime.
motivation: Multiphoton transitions are important for spectroscopy and quantum control; shaping the coherence of light can enhance these transitions.
method: The authors derive optimal coherence functions for the light field using a perturbative approach and solve the optimization problem analytically.
result: They find that the optimal field is a coherent state for one-photon transitions, but for higher-order transitions, the optimal field has non-classical coherence properties.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for enhancing multiphoton processes by engineering the coherence of light, with potential applications in quantum optics and spectroscopy.

motivation: Understanding the stability of superfluid currents in lattice models with long-range hopping is important for condensed matter physics, but the paper does not address quantum information or thermodynamic aspects.
method: The authors use mean-field theory and numerical simulations to analyze the Bose-Hubbard model with algebraically decaying hopping amplitudes on a square lattice.
result: They find that current-carrying states become unstable above a critical current, and the stability depends on the hopping range and interaction strength.

method: The authors analyze the dynamical bulk-edge relation analytically and numerically, examining how system size affects the power-law dependence and edge loss probability.
result: They find that finite-size effects modify the edge loss probability and the associated power-law scaling, with implications for the observability of the bulk-edge correspondence.

title: Tensor Network Loop Cluster Expansions For Quantum Many-body Problems

tldr: This paper analyzes tensor network loop cluster expansions as systematic corrections to belief propagation for quantum many-body problems.

result: The method yields systematic corrections to belief propagation, with numerical evidence of improved accuracy for certain quantum many-body problems.

title: Quantum Theory For Edge Current And Noise In Two-dimensional Topological Superconductors
authors: S. Pintus And A. Crépieux

tldr: This paper calculates edge current and noise in 2D topological superconductors using S-matrix and Green's function techniques.
motivation: To understand the properties of edge states in topological superconductors, particularly the distinction between chiral and nonchiral edge states via current and noise.
method: The authors employ S-matrix and Green's function techniques to compute edge current and its fluctuations.
result: The edge current is zero for nonchiral edge states and nonzero for chiral edge states, while edge noise is nonzero in both cases.
conclusion: Edge current and noise can serve as signatures to distinguish chiral from nonchiral edge states in topological superconductors.

This work provides explicit equations of motion for studying the real- and imaginary-time e…

motivation: To develop a numerically efficient method for simulating quantum systems with fermionic Gaussian states that can handle parity-violating interactions.
method: The authors derive equations of motion for parity-violating fermionic Gaussian states (PV-FGS) and apply them to real- and imaginary-time evolution.
result: They provide explicit equations of motion and demonstrate the method's applicability to general spin-1/2 Hamiltonians.
conclusion: The PV-FMFT offers a computationally efficient approach for studying fermionic systems with parity violation, relevant to condensed matter physics.

method: The authors use density matrix formalism combined with the finite difference time domain (FDTD) method to simulate pulse propagation.
result: They explore the effects of Rydberg blockade, including reduction of absorption and modification of pulse shape.
conclusion: The study provides insights into the dynamics of Rydberg excitons under strong interactions, but does not directly connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems as defined.

method: Matrix product states (MPS) are used to solve the Fermi-Hubbard model for non-bipartite ladders and extract effective spin Hamiltonians.
result: The study identifies accurate spin models that capture the low-energy physics of the system, including magnetic ordering and gaps.
conclusion: The approach provides a systematic way to derive spin models for complex carbon-based materials, aiding in the design of molecular magnets.

motivation: Understanding localization phenomena in non-Hermitian systems is of fundamental interest in condensed matter physics, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors analyze a one-dimensional non-Hermitian quasiperiodic chain with period-2 mosaic modulation and nonreciprocal hopping, using numerical and possibly analytical methods to study localization transitions.
result: They find that increasing hopping asymmetry induces a rich reentrant localization behavior, with multiple transitions between localized and delocalized phases.
conclusion: The work reveals complex localization physics in non-Hermitian quasiperiodic systems, but it is not aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

conclusion: Fractal geometries can modify universal transport features, but the work is primarily a condensed matter transport study without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

result: Provides a comparative analysis of accuracy and computational cost across methods for different parameter regimes.

motivation: To explore whether strong directional disorder in local magnetic moments can induce new topological phases in a Chern insulator, beyond what is possible in clean systems.

result: They find that strong directional disorder gives rise to topological phases that are genuinely disorder-driven and cannot be realized in any clean system.
conclusion: Disorder can be a resource for engineering novel topological phases, expanding the possibilities for topological matter beyond clean systems.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: A review of space-time duality in quantum many-body dynamics, focusing on brickwork quantum circuits and their analogy to quantum computation.
motivation: Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult; space-time duality offers a unified framework by treating space and time on equal footing.
method: The review discusses discretized time evolution on lattice systems, brickwork quantum circuits, and the space-time duality mapping to simplify dynamics.
result: It provides a pedagogical overview of how space-time duality relates to exactly solvable models and quantum circuit dynamics.
conclusion: Space-time duality provides a powerful tool for understanding and computing quantum many-body dynamics, with deep connections to quantum computation.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions

abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review of quantum aspects of magnetic skyrmions, covering their formation and quantum features.
motivation: Magnetic skyrmions are promising for spintronic applications, and understanding their quantum properties may enable new functionalities.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion quantum mechanics, including interactions and quantum tunneling.
result: It summarizes current understanding of quantum effects in skyrmions, such as quantum depinning and superposition states.
conclusion: Quantum skyrmionics is an emerging field with potential for future quantum technologies, but many open questions remain.

title: Quantum Cellular Automata On Symmetric Subalgebras
authors: Ruochen Ma, Yabo Li, And Meng Cheng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2123 (2026).

We investigate quantum cellular automata (QCA) on one-dimensional spin systems defined over a subalgebra of the full local operator algebra – the symmetric subalgebra under a finite Abelian group symmetry [MATH]. For systems where each site carries a regular representation of [MATH], we establish a complete classification of such subalgebra QCAs based on two topological invariants: (1) a surjective homomorphism from the group of subalgebra QCAs to the group of anyon permutation symmetries in a [MATH] [MATH] gauge theory; and (2) a generalization of the Gross-Nesme-Vogts-Werner (GNVW) index that characterizes the flow of the symmetric subalgebra. Specifically, two subalgebra QCAs correspond to the same anyon permutation and share the same index if and only if they differ by a finite-depth unitary circuit composed of [MATH]-symmetric local gates. We also identify a set of operations that generate all subalgebra QCAs through finite compositions. As an example, we examine the Kramers-Wannier duality on a [MATH] symmetric subalgebra, demonstrating that it maps to the [MATH]-[MATH] permutation in the two-dimensional toric code and has an irrational index of [MATH]. Therefore, it cannot be extended to a QCA over the full local operator algebra and mixes nontrivially with lattice translations.

.
tldr: Classifies quantum cellular automata on symmetric subalgebras using topological invariants and shows the Kramers-Wannier duality has an irrational index.
motivation: To understand the structure and classification of quantum cellular automata that respect a symmetry, which is important for understanding topological phases and dualities.
method: Uses algebraic methods to define subalgebra QCAs, computes invariants (anyon permutation and GNVW index), and shows equivalence to finite-depth circuits.
result: Establishes a complete classification of subalgebra QCAs for finite Abelian group symmetries, and demonstrates that the Kramers-Wannier duality cannot be extended to a full QCA.
conclusion: Subalgebra QCAs are classified by two invariants and are generated by a finite set of operations; the Kramers-Wannier duality is a nontrivial example with irrational index.

title: Squeezing Enhancement In Lossy Multi-Path Atom Interferometers
authors: Julian Günther, Jan-Niclas Kirsten-Siemß, Naceur Gaaloul, And Klemens Hammerer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2122 (2026).

This paper explores the sensitivity gains afforded by spin-squeezed states in atom interferometry, in particular using Bragg diffraction. We introduce a generalised input-output formalism that accurately describes realistic, non-unitary interferometers, including losses due to velocity selectivity and scattering into undesired momentum states. This formalism is applied to evaluate the performance of one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states in improving phase sensitivity. Our results show that by carefully optimising the parameters of the Bragg beam splitters and controlling the degree of squeezing, it is possible to improve the sensitivity of the interferometer by several dB with respect to the standard quantum limit despite realistic levels of losses in light pulse operations. However, the analysis also highlights the challenges associated with achieving these improvements in practice, most notably the impact of finite temperature on the benefits of entanglement. The results suggest ways of optimising interferometric setups to exploit quantum entanglement under realistic conditions, thereby contributing to advances in precision metrology with atom interferometers.

.
tldr: This paper studies sensitivity enhancement using spin-squeezed states in lossy multi-path atom interferometers, focusing on practical metrology rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Atom interferometers are limited by the standard quantum limit; spin-squeezed states can surpass it, but losses and finite temperature degrade performance. The paper aims to quantify realistic gains.
method: A generalized input-output formalism is developed to model non-unitary interferometers with losses from velocity selectivity and scattering. One-axis twisted spin-squeezed states are evaluated for phase sensitivity.
result: Optimizing Bragg beam splitter parameters and squeezing degree can yield several dB improvement over the standard quantum limit despite losses, but finite temperature significantly reduces the benefit.
conclusion: Quantum entanglement can enhance atom interferometry under realistic conditions, but practical challenges like temperature must be addressed to realize the gains.

title: Symmetry-induced Logarithmic Relaxation In The Quantum Kicked Rotor
authors: Julien Hébraud, Floriane Arrouas, Bruno Peaudecerf, Juliette Billy, David Guéry-Odelin, Olivier Giraud, Bertrand Georgeot, Gabriel Lemarié And Christian Miniatura
abstract: We study the effect of discrete symmetries on coherent multiple scattering in the quantum kicked rotor. When the initial momentum is set to zero—as in recent Bose–Einstein condensate experiments—the effective pseudo-disorder becomes even under momentum inversion. The resulting discrete mirror symmetry of the dynamics profoundly alters spectral correlations: it generates quasi-degenerate Floquet doublets localised at opposite momenta, whose exponentially small splittings produce a hierarchy of exponentially large dynamical timescales. The coherent backscattering and forward-scattering peaks then exhibit a striking non-monotonic evolution and strongly asymmetric contrasts, followed by an exceptionally slow logarithmic relaxation toward a common asymptotic value—a hallmark of glassy dynamics, here emerging in a fully coherent quantum system. That such archetypal glass-like behaviour arises from a single discrete symmetry constraint reveals an unexpected and deep connection between quantum coherence and slow relaxation phenomena.
tldr: This paper shows that discrete mirror symmetry in the quantum kicked rotor leads to logarithmic relaxation, a glassy dynamics signature, in a fully coherent quantum system.
motivation: To understand how discrete symmetries affect coherent multiple scattering and spectral correlations in quantum systems, and to explore the emergence of slow relaxation without disorder.
method: The authors study the quantum kicked rotor with zero initial momentum, analyze Floquet quasienergies and eigenstates, and compute coherent backscattering and forward-scattering peaks analytically and numerically.
result: Mirror symmetry creates quasi-degenerate Floquet doublets with exponentially small splittings, leading to non-monotonic evolution and logarithmic relaxation of scattering peaks.
conclusion: A single discrete symmetry can induce glassy dynamics in a coherent quantum system, revealing a deep connection between symmetry and slow relaxation.

title: Input-schema Identifiability Limits In Physics-informed Surrogates For Mechanics-governed Flow
authors: Andrzej Czyzewski Daniel Cieslak
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-informed and data-driven surrogates are increasingly used to approximate mechanics-governed flow fields, but the target quantities assigned to such models are not always identifiable from the input variables available at prediction time. We introduce an input-schema identifiability certificate for computational surrogates. Starting from a reduced physical model, the certificate decomposes a target field into components that are measurable from geometry, components that require boundary-condition information, and components identifiable only up to a symmetry quotient. This yields a pre-training audit: it predicts which oracle-channel interventions should reduce error, which should fail, and which ambiguity cannot be removed by changing the architecture, loss, optimizer, or sample size. We instantiate the framework for incompressible tubular flow using a Cosserat-rod reduction, where lumen velocity separates into a mesh-measurable tangent direction, a boundary-condition-dependent magnitude, and a signed-orientation ambiguity. Controlled experiments on patient-specific aortic CFD geometries, analytic Womersley flows, and an advection-diffusion transfer problem confirm the predicted pattern: supplying signed direction collapses angular error to the oracle regime, whereas supplying magnitude without orientation leaves the predicted sign ambiguity and yields 16-33 percent per-node sign flips. The results provide a mechanics-based diagnostic for deciding whether a surrogate modelling task is physically identifiable before training, and expose failure modes that aggregate error metrics can hide.
tldr: This paper introduces an input-schema identifiability certificate for physics-informed surrogates of mechanics-governed flow, focusing on which target field components are identifiable from input variables.
motivation: Physics-informed surrogates may fail to predict quantities that are not identifiable from available inputs, leading to hidden errors. The authors aim to provide a pre-training audit to diagnose such identifiability issues.
method: They develop a certificate based on a reduced physical model (Cosserat-rod reduction for tubular flow) that decomposes the target field into components measurable from geometry, boundary conditions, and symmetry-related ambiguities.
result: Experiments on aortic CFD geometries, Womersley flows, and advection-diffusion confirm that supplying signed direction collapses angular error, while magnitude without orientation leaves sign ambiguity causing 16-33% sign flips.
conclusion: The framework provides a mechanics-based diagnostic for identifiability before training, exposing failure modes that aggregate error metrics can hide.

title: Measuring A Quantum System Without Problems
authors: Marco Falconi, Clotilde Fermanian Kammerer, Rapha\"el Gautier
abstract: ArXiv:2606.21211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The process of measuring quantum observables has been plagued, since the inception of quantum mechanics, by the so-called measurement problem: it is impossible to read a definite outcome on a quantum scale. In this paper, we overcome this century-old problem by proving the existence of a measurement scheme in which the probe undergoes a quantum-to-classical transition, all the while satisfying the requirements of measurements in standard quantum mechanics.
tldr: The paper claims to solve the measurement problem by constructing a measurement scheme where the probe undergoes a quantum-to-classical transition.
motivation: The measurement problem has been a foundational issue in quantum mechanics; the authors aim to resolve it by proving the existence of a measurement scheme that yields definite outcomes.
method: The authors propose a mathematical framework for a measurement scheme that incorporates a quantum-to-classical transition, satisfying standard quantum measurement postulates.
result: They claim to have proven the existence of such a scheme, thereby overcoming the measurement problem.
conclusion: The paper asserts a resolution to the measurement problem, but the approach is highly abstract and not connected to practical quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Mitigating Outages In A 4.6-km Fso Link Via Mode-Diverse Reception: An Experimentally Validated Digital Twin Approach
authors: Jonas Krimmer, Vincent van Vliet, Menno van Den Hout, Eduward Tangdiongga, Chigo Okonkwo, Sebastian Randel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.21341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Terrestrial coherent FSO requires mitigating turbulence-induced coupling losses. We experimentally validate a "Digital Twin" channel model against fading statistics from a 4.6-km link. Combining long-term scintillometer data with mode-diverse receiver simulations, we demonstrate that a 6-mode receiver reduces turbulence-induced outage probabilities to 2.02e-5.
tldr: This paper experimentally validates a digital twin channel model for a 4.6-km free-space optical link and demonstrates that mode-diverse reception reduces turbulence-induced outage probabilities.
motivation: Terrestrial coherent free-space optical (FSO) communication suffers from turbulence-induced coupling losses, and mitigating outages is critical for reliable links.
method: The authors combine long-term scintillometer data with mode-diverse receiver simulations to build a digital twin channel model, validated against fading statistics from a 4.6-km FSO link.
result: A 6-mode receiver reduces turbulence-induced outage probabilities to 2.02e-5.
conclusion: Mode-diverse reception is an effective technique to mitigate outages in terrestrial FSO links, and the digital twin approach accurately models the channel.

title: QVaR: A Quantum Variational Regularization Method For Linear Inverse Problems
authors: Siiri Rautio, Hj{\o}rdis Schl\"uter, Andreas Hauptmann, Babak Maboudi Afkham
abstract: ArXiv:2606.21392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a tailored framework for solving regularized linear inverse problems using quantum optimization methods. By discretizing the solution space and encoding data fidelity and regularization terms into quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) models, we formulate both Tikhonov- and sparsity-promoting regularized inverse problems within a unified quantum optimization framework. We further introduce a notion of quantum sensitivity that characterizes the effect of perturbations arising from approximate quantum evolution and discretization. We derive bounds relating these perturbations to stability properties of the underlying inverse problem, thereby establishing a theoretical connection between quantum solution variability and classical notions of ill-posedness. The framework is extended to variational inverse problems through wavelet-based representations and complemented by reduced-order modeling strategies in both parameter and Hamiltonian spaces to mitigate current hardware limitations. Numerical experiments on simulated and physical quantum hardware indicate that the resulting low-energy solution distributions retain information about the underlying inverse problem, while also revealing the limitations imposed by finite-time evolution, discretization, and hardware noise.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum variational regularization method for solving linear inverse problems using QUBO formulations and quantum optimization.
motivation: Classical inverse problems are often ill-posed and require regularization; quantum optimization may offer advantages for certain discretized formulations.
method: The authors discretize the solution space and encode Tikhonov and sparsity-promoting regularization into QUBO models, then solve them using quantum variational methods. They introduce a notion of quantum sensitivity to analyze perturbations.

title: Reformulation Invariance And The Axiomatic Foundations Of Inference
authors: Rapha\"el Tr\'esor, Thijs van de Laar, Bert de Vries
abstract: ArXiv:2606.21551v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Maximum entropy, Bayesian updating, and exponential-family estimation are all instances of a common inference principle: selecting the measure or distribution that minimizes a divergence subject to the available constraints. Which divergence to use is usually decided by analytic convenience, by empirical performance, or by a set of axioms chosen to single it out, leaving open a basic question: why one divergence and not another? We answer it from a single requirement: an inference method should return the same answer whenever the same problem is presented in an equivalent form, for instance, after simply renaming its parts. This requirement alone forces inference to be the minimisation of a classical divergence, and each further reformulation it must respect tightens the admissible family one notch, narrowing the broad f-divergences to the {\alpha}-divergences and finally to the single Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. Mathematically, inference is recast from minimising a numerical functional to selecting a least element under a preorder on positive measures, a divergence being merely one numerical scale that reproduces that preorder. The reformulations are the morphisms of a category of inference problems, and the invariance requirement says the inference operator is a covariant functor into the category of statistical models of Cencov, mirroring his characterisation of the Fisher metric. The representation is proved on finite spaces and lifted to general measurable spaces by an elementary closure, covering discrete and continuous spaces alike. Earlier axiomatisations, such as those of Shore-Johnson and Csiszar, postulate their consistency axioms directly and only on finite alphabets; here the axioms follow from reformulation invariance alone.
tldr: The paper derives inference principles (maximum entropy, Bayesian updating) from a requirement of reformulation invariance, using category theory and preorders on measures.
motivation: To answer why specific divergences (e.g., KL divergence) are used in inference, rather than others, by grounding the choice in a single invariance principle.
method: The authors formalize inference as selecting a least element under a preorder on positive measures, with reformulations as morphisms in a category; they prove that invariance forces minimization of f-divergences, then α-divergences, then KL divergence.
result: Reformulation invariance alone forces inference to minimize a classical divergence; additional invariance constraints narrow the family to KL divergence. The representation is proved on finite spaces and lifted to general measurable spaces.
conclusion: The axiomatic foundations of inference can be derived from a single requirement of reformulation invariance, unifying maximum entropy, Bayesian updating, and exponential-family estimation.

In this note we prove that extension is just a particular three-dimensional instance of a general family of second order mixed moment inequalities based on Gram matrices of arbitrary random vectors. We also discuss some implications of these inequalities on Cramer-Rao lower bound for biased estimators.
tldr: The paper extends a known inequality for random variables to a general family of second order mixed moment inequalities based on Gram matrices, with applications to Cramér-Rao bounds.
motivation: To generalize a recent extension of Walker's inequality and explore its implications for biased estimators.

conclusion: The inequalities provide a unified framework for certain moment bounds and may have applications in estimation theory.

title: Operator Inequalities In $\Phi$-Product Tensor Algebras: Invariance And Transform Sensitivity
authors: Michael K. Ng Shih-Yu Chang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.21667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study classical operator inequalities in [MATH]-product tensor algebras (a transformation [MATH]-based generalization of the [MATH]-product framework) for third-order tensors. Although these algebras are algebraically isomorphic under different unitary transforms [MATH], we show that their quantitative behavior is not invariant. We prove that fundamental inequalities, including Golden--Thompson, Jensen, Klein, and Lieb, extend to the [MATH]-product setting with the same constants as in the matrix case. However, the associated defect -- the slack between the two sides of the inequality -- depends explicitly on transform-domain noncommutativity. In particular, we establish a sharp characterization of the defect in terms of slice-wise commutators, revealing that inequality tightness is governed by transform-induced noncommutativity. We further demonstrate strong transform sensitivity by constructing explicit tensor pairs for which the defect vanishes under one transform (e.g., discrete Fourier transform) but grows linearly with the tensor depth under another transform (e.g., discrete Cosine transform), yielding an [MATH] separation where [MATH] is the matrix dimension of [MATH]. Moreover, we prove that no transform is universally optimal: for any pair of transforms, there exist tensors for which each is strictly better than the other. These results show that the choice of transform defines a coordinate system in which commutativity is measured, inducing a nontrivial geometry of inequality tightness. Consequently, optimal transform selection is inherently data-dependent and can be formulated as an optimization problem over the unitary group.
tldr: This paper studies operator inequalities in Φ-product tensor algebras for third-order tensors, showing that inequality tightness depends on the choice of unitary transform.
motivation: To understand how classical operator inequalities extend to tensor algebras and how the choice of transform affects their quantitative behavior.
method: The authors prove extensions of Golden–Thompson, Jensen, Klein, and Lieb inequalities to the Φ-product setting and analyze the defect in terms of slice-wise commutators.
result: Inequality tightness is governed by transform-induced noncommutativity; no transform is universally optimal, and the defect can vary by an O(n) factor between transforms.
conclusion: Optimal transform selection is data-dependent and can be formulated as an optimization problem over the unitary group.
